scenario:
A mid-sized Czech bank (about 2,500 employees) has had an enterprise architecture team for three years. The team has built an extensive model of the current state of all applications and processes in a modelling tool and published a set of architecture principles. Projects and product owners nevertheless almost never turn to the team. Investments are decided by a change portfolio committee to which architects are not invited, and architects learn about new initiatives only once a supplier has been selected and the contract signed.
The new CIO is considering disbanding the team because, in their view, it “does not bring value”. In four months, preparation of next year's budget begins, in which large investments in digital channels and the replacement of core banking will be decided. The CIO has asked you, as the new lead architect, for a proposal on how the enterprise architecture practice should work so that it genuinely helps the bank.
question: Which approach best corresponds to the TOGAF Standard and addresses the bank's situation?
options: Together with the CIO as sponsor, connect architecture to the bank's decision-making cycle: for the budget preparation, develop an architecture supporting strategy and portfolio for digital channels and core banking, with options, benefits, risks and a roadmap. Establish an Architecture Board with a leadership mandate and include an architecture assessment in investment approval, so that architecture is used before the decision is made.

Focus the team on the upcoming budget preparation: the architects alone develop an architecture supporting strategy and portfolio for digital channels and core banking, with options, benefits, risks and a roadmap, and send it to the change portfolio committee as a recommendation. Postpone executive sponsorship and the establishment of an Architecture Board until the team proves its value with concrete results and gains the CIO's trust.

Introduce mandatory compliance reviews of all projects against the published principles and the current-state model, and stipulate that a project without a positive architect assessment may not accept delivery from a supplier. Handle deviations through dispensations granted by the architecture team, and report the level of project compliance to the CIO once a quarter so that the value the team brings is visible.

First complete and refine the current-state model of all domains down to the level of individual interfaces and acquire a more powerful repository tool with a publishing portal, so that the team has a complete and trustworthy Architecture Landscape. Approach projects and the committee only with the finished model, because without a complete and verified baseline it is not possible to recommend investments in digital channels or in the replacement of core banking in a qualified way.
explanation: According to TOGAF (G186), the purpose of enterprise architecture is to guide effective change, and it brings value only when it is used in decision-making in the business and budget cycle – the best answer therefore targets the budget preparation while also ensuring sponsorship and governance through the Architecture Board. The second option has the right focus, but without a sponsor and a mandate there is a risk that nobody will use the recommendation again. The third option uses governance tools, but only after the decision, as enforcement; moreover, dispensations are granted by the Architecture Board, not by the architecture team. The last option repeats the original mistake: detailed documentation without a purpose that misses the decision window.

scenario:
A health insurance company is introducing a unified interface for data exchange with healthcare providers. The Architecture Requirements Specification and the Architecture Definition Document stipulate, among other things, mandatory publication of services through a central API gateway, unified user authentication and a standardised message data format. The Architecture Board has asked the lead architect for a quarterly compliance report on the three projects that implement the specification.
The portal for providers implemented all elements of the specification exactly as specified and, in addition, added its own caching layer, which the specification does not address at all. The mobile application for policyholders has so far implemented only some of the specified elements (the rest is planned for the next release), but everything it implemented corresponds to the specification and it added nothing extra. The internal reporting application does use the standard message format, but accesses the data directly in the database, bypassing the API gateway, which is in conflict with the specification. The project managers are pushing for the report to come across as favourably as possible.
question: How should the lead architect evaluate the results according to the TOGAF Standard, and what should they recommend?
options: Evaluate the portal as Conformant, the mobile application as Compliant and reporting as Non-conformant. Leave the decision on remediation of reporting, or on a time-limited dispensation, to the Architecture Board, because exceptions are approved by governance; for the portal, assess the risk of the caching layer and the extension of the specification, and for the mobile application, monitor the delivery of the missing elements, so that the Board has a complete picture.

Evaluate the portal as Conformant, the mobile application as Compliant and reporting as Non-conformant, and submit to the Architecture Board a proposal for remediation or a time-limited dispensation for reporting. Propose no further measures for the portal and the mobile application: nothing they implemented is in conflict with the specification, so monitoring them further is not necessary.

Evaluate the portal as Compliant, because beyond the specification it added its own elements (the caching layer), and the mobile application as Conformant, because everything it implemented corresponds to the specification; reporting as Non-conformant. Recommend to the Architecture Board remediation or a time-limited dispensation with conditions for reporting, and for the other two projects monitor their further development according to the roadmap.

Evaluate reporting as Consistent, because it uses the standard message format, and present all three projects to the Architecture Board as compliant with the architecture. Direct database access is an internal technical decision of the project that does not materially change the specification, and if the Board were to raise it, it can be justified retrospectively in the Compliance Assessment.
explanation: According to the TOGAF compliance levels, the portal is Conformant (it implements everything from the specification plus elements that the specification does not cover), the mobile application is Compliant (it implements only part, but everything in accordance with the specification) and reporting is Non-conformant (an element of the specification is implemented in conflict with it). The best answer classifies correctly, leaves the decision on remediation or a time-limited dispensation to the Architecture Board, and also addresses the risks of the added elements and the completion of the missing ones. The second option classifies correctly but omits the necessary further measures for the portal and the mobile application. The third confuses the classic Compliant/Conformant pair, and the last option conceals the non-conformance and bypasses governance.

scenario:
The merger of two regional distribution companies (electricity and gas) created a group of approximately 4,000 employees. One company had a small enterprise architecture department that worked according to TOGAF and had its own Architecture Board; the other had only a few solution architects scattered across projects, with no common principles. The two companies have different ERP and customer systems, and people in both IT departments fear whose approach will “win”. The group manages projects according to PRINCE2, runs IT operations according to ITIL and has an established enterprise risk management framework; energy regulation, moreover, requires separation of distribution data from trading data.
The Group CIO has appointed you chief architect with the task of building a unified architecture practice for the whole group. In six months a large integration programme is to begin (unification of customer systems, GIS and network management), and management expects architecture to support and guide it.
question: Which approach is most appropriate according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Because this is a new enterprise, carry out the Preliminary Phase. In it, define the organisations affected, confirm the links to PRINCE2, ITIL, risk management and regulation, establish the team and the Organizational Model for EA, define Architecture Principles and prepare a Tailored Architecture Framework. Establish an Architecture Governance Framework with a single Architecture Board, set up partitioning and establish the repository.

Adopt unchanged the practice of the company that already worked according to TOGAF, including its principles, templates, repository and Architecture Board, and extend it to the whole group. Integrate the second company's solution architects into its team and start Phase A of the integration programme straight away with this practice, without losing time on new set-up that would merely repeat work already done and proven.

Start Phase A of the integration programme straight away with the existing architects from both companies and define the architecture practice (roles, governance, principles) gradually according to the programme's needs. The group CIO prepares the Request for Architecture Work, and the integration programme steering committee temporarily serves as the Architecture Board until the permanent arrangement of the architecture function in the group is decided.

First acquire a unified EA tool, define a detailed metamodel and templates in it, and order all projects of both companies to document their systems, interfaces, data flows and processes in it. Postpone governance, principles and the allocation of responsibilities until the tool is populated and the model makes clear what the merged group really looks like and where the overlaps are.
explanation: Building an Architecture Capability for a newly formed enterprise is the task of the Preliminary Phase: defining the organisations affected, confirming links to other management frameworks, the Organizational Model for EA, principles, tailoring the framework, governance and the initial repository – which is what the best answer does. Adopting one company's practice sensibly uses existing assets, but omits tailoring to the new enterprise, its frameworks and regulatory requirements. Starting Phase A without an established capability and with provisional governance is a weak solution. Starting with a tool and blanket documentation without governance and principles contradicts the TOGAF approach.

scenario:
A Czech parcel delivery company (about 6,000 employees, fast growth thanks to e-commerce) has no formal architecture governance. This year the company is investing in automation of its sorting centres and a new application for parcel recipients, and the number of IT projects has doubled in two years. In practice, whether a project “gets through” is decided personally by the lead architect – sometimes stopping the project, at other times approving an exception, without justifying the decision or recording it anywhere. Division directors complain that architects block projects without explanation, and some disputes are settled directly with the CEO outside any process. The same exceptions (for example local data storage outside the central data platform) are repeatedly granted to different projects, and nobody has an overview of how many of them are in force and until when.
The CEO wants to put things right and has asked the lead architect for a proposal on how to set up architecture governance.
question: Which proposal best corresponds to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Establish an Architecture Board with a leadership mandate and representation of key business and IT stakeholders, and separate the roles: architects assess and recommend, the Board decides and handles escalations. Record decisions with their justification in the Governance Repository and set criteria for time-limited dispensations and their tracking, so that it is clear how many exceptions are in force and until when.

Establish an Architecture Board with a leadership mandate, in which key business and IT stakeholders are represented, and escalate disputed cases to it instead of to the CEO. Capture decisions briefly in meeting minutes; there is no need to introduce special criteria for exceptions or their recording and tracking, because the Board will assess each case individually according to its circumstances.

Establish an Architecture Board composed of the lead architect and domain architects, which will vote on projects and record its decisions, including justification, in the Governance Repository. Division directors will be informed of the voting results and the Board will grant exceptions according to the professional judgement of the architects, who know the target architecture and its context in detail.

Abolish architecture approval of projects so that it does not slow the company's growth, and transfer decision-making on solutions fully to the division directors, who know their business's needs best. Architects will be available as advisers on request, and any disputes between divisions will continue to be decided by the CEO according to the current business situation.
explanation: TOGAF requires explicit roles and decision rights: architects assess and advise, and an authorised body decides – the Architecture Board with a leadership mandate and representation of key stakeholders. Governance should be transparent and disciplined, so the best answer introduces recording of decisions in the Governance Repository, criteria for time-limited dispensations and an escalation path. The second option has the right Architecture Board structure but does not address the lack of transparency and the repeated exceptions, which are the core of the problem. A Board composed only of architects leaves decision-making to architects and does not represent the business; abolishing governance contradicts TOGAF.

scenario:
A supermarket retail chain in the Czech Republic and Slovakia has an approved segment architecture “Customer and Loyalty”. It stipulates that customer data is held exclusively in the central customer platform (master data) and that data exchange takes place through the enterprise integration platform. The Architecture Board approved it a year ago, among other reasons because of problems with inconsistent data in previous marketing campaigns. The project for a new mobile loyalty application has a fixed launch date before the Christmas season. The project architect has found that connecting to the integration platform takes about ten weeks because of the request queue, which will jeopardise the deadline.
The application supplier proposes holding customer profiles in its SaaS solution and synchronising them with the central platform once a day in a batch. Both the project manager and the marketing director (the project's sponsor) want the project architect to “approve” this solution, because in their view it is only a temporary measure.
question: How should the project architect proceed according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Assess the deviation against the segment architecture and, with the supplier and the owner of the segment, prepare options with impacts and risks – that is, a temporary solution with a deadline and a plan for returning to compliance, or an accelerated connection. Leave the decision to the Architecture Board, because the project cannot grant an exception from a superior architecture; the Board can grant a time-limited dispensation or initiate a change of the architecture.

Submit the supplier's solution to the Architecture Board as a request for a time-limited dispensation, because according to the sponsor it is a temporary measure. Do not examine other options or the impacts on the central customer platform and do not involve the owner of the segment architecture, because the Board will decide on the exception anyway and the pre-Christmas deadline does not allow a longer analysis.

Reject the supplier's solution, because the segment architecture is binding for the project, and insist on connecting through the integration platform (even at the cost of postponing the launch until after Christmas). Recommend that the project manager negotiate the postponement with the sponsor; no escalation or assessment of options is needed, because the rules of the segment architecture are unambiguous and approved by the Architecture Board.

Approve the supplier's solution, because the pre-Christmas deadline is key for the business and daily synchronisation with the central platform preserves data consistency, at least with a one-day delay. The segment architecture can be updated later to reflect the actual state, once the application is in operation and it is clear whether the temporary solution has proved itself.
explanation: Work at a lower level (project architecture) must respect the constraints of the superior (segment) architecture, and conflicts are resolved through governance, not at project level. The best answer analyses the deviation, prepares options with impacts and lets the Architecture Board decide – it can grant a time-limited dispensation or launch a change of the architecture. The second option chooses the right path via the Board, but without an analysis of options, impacts and a plan for return, and without the owner of the segment architecture, so the Board lacks the basis for a qualified decision. The third option respects the architecture but ignores the business need and the possibility of a controlled exception; the last option quietly accepts the deviation and bypasses governance.

scenario:
A pharmaceutical distributor with warehouses in Prague, Brno and Ostrava had a Target Architecture for warehouse management and order processing approved two years ago, built on extending its own on-premise ERP. Since then, the architecture team has regularly carried out compliance reviews of projects against this target architecture; a project for new warehouse scanning is currently under way, as well as a project to extend the ERP with a module for hospital pharmacies, which has a budget of CZK 25 million and has only just started implementation.
A month ago the board of directors announced that the company will join an international group and within three years will move to the group's cloud ERP; the group's detailed requirements are not yet known. The leaders of both projects insist that their projects are fully compliant with the target architecture and want to continue as planned.
question: How should the lead architect best proceed according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Alert the Architecture Board to the need to first verify whether the Target Architecture is still valid after the change of strategy, and propose its revision through a Change Request or a new Request for Architecture Work. In the meantime, together with the Board, reassess the running projects. Continue with what retains value after the move to the group ERP, and pause the extension of the on-premise ERP, because it is an investment without a future.

Alert the Architecture Board that the change of strategy requires a revision of the Target Architecture, and propose starting a new architecture cycle through a Request for Architecture Work. In the meantime, continue to assess the running projects against the existing approved target architecture, because it remains the binding basis for governance until the Board formally changes it, and projects may continue according to it.

Continue the compliance reviews of both projects against the existing Target Architecture, because it is formally approved and the projects comply with it, and record the change of strategy in the Compliance Assessment as a risk. Open the revision of the target architecture only once the group hands over its detailed requirements for the new ERP and it is exactly clear what needs to change.

Suspend compliance reviews until the situation is clarified and give the projects a free hand in design, budget and technology selection, because assessing against an outdated target architecture makes no sense. Derive the new target architecture directly from the group ERP (once the group publishes its standards), adopting its modules, processes, interfaces and data model, and then align the running projects with it retrospectively.
explanation: According to G186, architecture governance poses two questions: is the Target Architecture still valid and appropriate, and are the implementation projects compliant with it? With a fundamental change of strategy the first question must be addressed first – revise the target through the Board and at the same time reassess the projects so as not to invest in a state with no future, which is what the best answer does. The second option rightly launches the revision, but in the meantime lets projects build towards an outdated target. The third option postpones the question of the target's validity and merely records a risk; the last option abolishes governance entirely and leaves projects without direction.

scenario:
A Czech online retailer of electronics and household goods has 25 agile teams organised into tribes. Before every sprint, each team must submit its solution design to the Architecture Board; approval takes around three weeks, and the teams therefore work around architecture. Six architects spend most of their time preparing materials for the Board. As a result, over the last two years four different payment gateway integrations have emerged, customer data is duplicated in several services and technical debt is growing rapidly.
Management has approved the strategic goal of entering the Slovak and Polish markets within 18 months. The CTO claims that architecture is a brake and that agile teams do not need it; the CFO, on the contrary, demands that investments in the expansion be controlled and that no further duplication arise. The lead architect is to propose how enterprise architecture should support agile delivery.
question: Which approach is most appropriate according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: At the strategy and portfolio level, create for the expansion a target architecture, principles and guardrails for a single payment platform and ownership of customer data, and from them a backlog of work packages. Provide teams with architecture “just enough, just in time” in iterations and leave to the Board only shared platforms and deviations from the guardrails, because approving every sprint is a bottleneck.

Abolish approval before every sprint, publish principles and guardrails (e.g. one payment platform, ownership of customer data) and embed architects directly in the tribes so that they continuously create “just enough” architecture with the teams. Do not create a target architecture or a roadmap for the expansion, because it would quickly become outdated and the agile teams will derive the necessary steps themselves from the product backlog.

Keep approval by the Architecture Board before every sprint, but speed it up by introducing weekly meetings and uniform design templates. Before continuing the expansion, first create a detailed target design of all domains for the whole 18 months ahead, so that teams have a clear and complete brief and no further duplication can arise.

Give in to the CTO: abolish enterprise architecture and the Architecture Board and leave architecture entirely to emergent design in the individual teams, who know their services and customers first-hand. Address duplication and technical debt later with a separate consolidation project, once the expansion into the Slovak and Polish markets is complete, so that consolidation does not jeopardise the market entry date.
explanation: TOGAF supports agility in that architecture at different levels of detail gives agile teams context: the strategic and portfolio level determines the goal, principles, guardrails and a backlog of work packages, while architecture for delivery is created iteratively and “just in time” with the teams. The best answer combines both and focuses governance only on significant decisions. The second option rightly removes the bottleneck, but without a target architecture and a roadmap it ensures neither coordination of the expansion nor the CFO's requirement. The third option retains cumbersome gates and up-front waterfall design; abolishing architecture contradicts the purpose of EA and would only deepen the duplication problem.

scenario:
A non-life insurer is consolidating three policy administration systems; it is its largest investment in the last ten years and the Architecture Board monitors it every month. The architecture repository holds side by side: a model of the current state, a target architecture approved by the Architecture Board (one consolidated system with integration via an API layer), two transition architectures for 2026 and 2027, and two options presented by suppliers at workshops (a SaaS core and a low-code platform). The models and diagrams do not indicate which state they represent or whether they have been approved.
The project team for a new web portal for brokers proposed an integration based on the supplier's SaaS option, because it considered it to be the target. At the same time, the sales director asks why two different presentations show him two different roadmaps.
question: What should the lead architect do according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Mark in the repository for each architecture its state (candidate, current, transition, target), status and version, and keep the supplier options as candidates until a governance decision. Align the roadmap with the transition architectures, so that the sales director gets one valid version, and let the Architecture Board decide on the portal integration's deviation from the approved target.

Mark in the repository for each architecture its state (candidate, current, transition, target), status and version, label the supplier options as candidates and align the roadmap with the transition architectures. Inform the portal project team of the valid target and leave it to them to adjust the integration in one of the later releases according to their capacity and priorities, when it suits the portal.

Remove the supplier options from the repository so that they do not confuse, and keep in it only the current state and the approved target architecture, which are the only ones relevant for decision-making. Keep the transition architectures separately in project documentation and explain to the sales director that only the target architecture is binding, not the partial roadmaps of individual projects.

Given that the portal already counts on integration based on the SaaS option and the supplier regards it as promising, declare this option (the SaaS core) the new target architecture and adjust the roadmap, transition architectures and programme plan accordingly. The inconsistency between the presentations disappears, the sales director gets one roadmap and the project does not have to rework its design.
explanation: G186 recommends explicitly managing multiple architecture states – candidate (options to be assessed), current, transition and target – and holding them in the repository with a status and version so that roadmaps remain coherent. The best answer introduces this and at the same time uses governance to address the project that builds on an unapproved option. The second option removes the cause but leaves the existing deviation without a controlled assessment. Removing the candidate options and pushing transition architectures out of the repository loses important information and does not unify the roadmap; declaring an unapproved option the target merely because the implementer has already used it contradicts governance.

scenario: A group of three regional hospitals has launched a programme for a new integrated clinical system and a patient portal. In it, patients are to see test results and outpatient doctors discharge reports; the programme is at the beginning of Phase A and the portal is to be launched within 18 months. The architecture work plan assumes that the security team will be involved only in Phase G, in the form of penetration tests before launch. The CISO is not a member of the programme steering committee and the risk appetite is not defined anywhere. Hospital management sees security mainly as a cost item, even though ransomware attacks have hit several Czech hospitals in recent years and the group falls under the new cybersecurity obligations (NIS2). The IT director asks the lead architect how to correctly incorporate security into the architecture work.
question: Which approach is most appropriate according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Treat security as a cross-cutting concern and involve the CISO as a key stakeholder from the start. Agree the risk appetite and security principles with management, because the level of acceptable risk is determined by the business, and carry out the corresponding security activities in every ADM phase and domain. Present security not merely as a cost but as a condition for achieving the programme's benefits.

Involve the CISO as a key stakeholder from the start of the programme and add corresponding security activities in every ADM phase and domain, from risk assessment to security services. Leave the level of acceptable risk to the assessment of IT and the security team, because hospital management lacks sufficient expertise for such decisions and would decide mainly on the basis of cost.

Keep the penetration tests in Phase G and additionally include at the end of Phase D a security review of the technology architecture that verifies firewalls, encryption, network segmentation and backup. Add the security requirements from this review to the Architecture Requirements Specification before suppliers are selected, so that suppliers have to meet them.

Transfer responsibility for security contractually to the suppliers of the clinical system and the portal, who have certifications, experience from other hospitals and their own security team, and do not address it further in the architecture. Involve the hospitals' security team only in operations, where it is to monitor incidents, evaluate logs and coordinate the response with suppliers.
explanation: G152 views security as a cross-cutting concern of all domains, phases and stakeholders, and Enterprise Security Architecture integrates information security management and enterprise risk management into EA; building security in from the start is cheaper than adding it afterwards. The best answer also addresses the missing risk appetite, which must be set by the business (management), and presents security as a condition for the benefits. The second option has the right involvement of the CISO and activities across phases, but wrongly shifts the decision on acceptable risk to IT. A review only at the end of Phase D is late and purely technological; transferring security to suppliers contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: An energy company (electricity sales and distribution) is preparing a programme of dynamic tariffs and a data platform for smart meter data; competitors already offer dynamic tariffs. The steering committee, attended by the sales director, the distribution director and the CIO, demands that before approval architecture “eliminate all risks”. An option with an analytics platform in the public cloud, which promises significantly faster time to market for the tariffs and lower costs, was rejected at the last meeting as “risky” without anyone comparing the risks and benefits. The risk appetite is not defined, risks in the programme are recorded only as a list of threats maintained by the project office, and the enterprise risk management manager complains that they were not invited to the programme. The lead architect is to prepare materials for the decision on the option.
question: How should the lead architect approach risk management according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Understand risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, including opportunities, and agree the risk appetite with management and enterprise risk management, because “eliminating all risks” is not possible. For each option, assess the initial risk, propose mitigation and determine the residual risk; present the options with benefits and residual risks to the steering committee for decision and acceptance, and keep monitoring the risks.

For each option, carry out risk classification and identification, assess the initial risk, propose mitigation and determine the residual risk, which the steering committee formally accepts, and monitor the risks continuously. Assess only threats and possible losses, because the task of risk management is to protect the programme from negative impacts; the benefits of the options are a matter for the business case, not risk management.

Recommend the option with the on-premise platform as the least risky, because it corresponds to the steering committee's requirement, and document its residual risks in the Architecture Definition Document. Which residual risks are acceptable will be decided by the lead architect, because they have the best overview of the technical context of both options and of the possibilities for their mitigation.

Leave risk management to the project office, which already maintains the list of threats and has an established process, templates and tool for it, and focus architecture on the technical design of both options, their costs and schedule. Address risks in detail only in Phase G, when the suppliers and specific technologies will be known and the risks can be exactly quantified and assigned to owners.
explanation: G152 extends risk management with the ERM perspective: risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives (positive and negative) and the goal is to maximise benefit and minimise loss within the bounds of the risk appetite. The best answer therefore includes opportunities, agrees the risk appetite and presents decision makers with the initial and residual risks together with the benefits; residual risks are accepted by governance. The second option carries out the TOGAF risk management process correctly but sees only threats, and without a risk appetite cannot fairly compare the cloud opportunity. The third option leaves risk acceptance to the architect and promises the “lowest risk” instead of balancing; the last option removes risk from architecture entirely.

scenario: A Czech fintech company offering deferred payments and payment accounts was founded four years ago. It has 180 employees, 110 of them in development, and its products run in the public cloud. From the original two development teams it now has fourteen product teams, and in nine months it wants to apply for a banking licence. Architecture has so far been determined informally by the founder and CTO; teams now choose technologies on their own and incompatible solutions are emerging. Some of the developers came from banks and associate architecture rules with slow approval processes. In the licensing procedure the regulator will require evidence of IT governance, risk management and accountabilities. At the same time, the founders insist that the company must not lose the speed that distinguishes it from banks. The CTO has hired the first enterprise architect and asks them how architecture should work in the company.
question: Which approach is most appropriate according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Tailor EA to a company that is growing from a few teams into a network of teams and heading towards a regulated institution. Offer EA as services, including design support with Minimum Viable Architecture, set a small set of principles, guardrails and shared platforms, and according to the licence schedule gradually add formal governance, risk management and compliance, so that the company can demonstrate them to the regulator.

Offer EA as services (e.g. design support with Minimum Viable Architecture) and for coordinating the fourteen teams set a small set of principles, guardrails and shared platforms, so that the company does not lose speed. Introduce formal governance, risk management and compliance only when the regulator explicitly requests them in the licensing procedure, so that advance preparations do not slow down product development.

Introduce TOGAF in full, just as in an established bank: for every initiative produce a complete set of ADM deliverables and have every change approved by the Architecture Board. The regulator will thus see mature governance and teams will get clear and uniform rules, even though product delivery slows down for several months.

Keep the existing informal model in which architecture is determined by the founder and CTO, because it is precisely this that gave the company its speed and competitive advantage. For the licensing procedure, have documentation of architecture, governance and accountabilities produced retrospectively, exactly according to the regulator's requirements, so that the application passes as soon as possible, and update it once a year with the help of external consultants.
explanation: TOGAF assumes tailoring of the enterprise's architecture practice and offers EA as services, e.g. design support including Minimum Viable Architecture; G217 describes the role of EA in contexts from a founder through a team and a network of teams to a lasting enterprise, with the need for coordination growing with the number of teams. The best answer combines light-touch coordination with introducing formal governance, risk and compliance according to the needs of the licence. The second option handles team coordination and speed well, but addresses the regulatory requirement, which is critical for the company, only reactively instead of planning governance according to the licence schedule. Full introduction of all deliverables and approval of every change would show the regulator formal governance, but it is untailored and sacrifices the speed the founders insist on; documentation written retrospectively just for the regulator contradicts the purpose of EA.

scenario: A chain of 300 pharmacies in the Czech Republic is launching an omnichannel programme: reserving medicines in an app, pick-up at a branch, a unified stock overview and better integration with eRecept (the electronic prescription system). The pilot is to start in a year and the sponsor is the sales director. The lead architect has so far held initial workshops only with the heads of the IT department and with the e-commerce director. Not involved were the head pharmacists and branch operations, logistics and the central warehouse, the finance department, franchise partners operating about a third of the pharmacies, the data protection officer and the external payment gateway provider. The franchisees have their own checkout systems and contractually reserve the right to consent to changes that affect their operations. At the last management meeting they voiced objections that the programme is “run by IT without them”, and the head pharmacists point to impacts on work at the dispensing counters. The programme is at the beginning of Phase A.
question: How should the lead architect now proceed in stakeholder management according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Identify stakeholders in all groups, from management and finance through branch operations and logistics to franchisees, the data protection officer and external partners, and their concerns, classify their positions and determine the way of engaging them using the power/interest grid. Capture the result in the Stakeholder Map, choose suitable viewpoints for the groups and derive the Communications Plan from it.

Identify and classify stakeholders using the power/interest grid and capture them in the Stakeholder Map. Immediately engage the Key Players actively – management, IT and the franchisees with the contractual right of consent – and approach the other groups (branch operations, logistics, finance, the data protection officer and the payment gateway provider) later in Phase B, when it will be clear how exactly the solution will affect them.

Send all department heads and franchisees a questionnaire asking them to submit their requirements for the omnichannel solution and merge the answers into a single list of requirements for the Statement of Architecture Work. Then regularly send the same list and the programme status to all groups by e-mail, so that everyone has the same information and nobody feels left out.

Continue working with IT and e-commerce, who understand the technical solution best, and inform the other groups only after the Architecture Vision is approved, so that the programme's scope is not needlessly extended. Pass the objections of the franchisees and head pharmacists to the sales director, who as sponsor will resolve them within their authority and business relationships.
explanation: The Stakeholder Management technique in TOGAF begins with identifying all stakeholders and their concerns, continues with classifying positions, determining the approach according to the power/interest grid and tailoring the outputs (viewpoints); the result is the Stakeholder Map, from which the Communications Plan is derived – this is what the best answer contains. The second option begins the technique correctly and rightly places the franchisees among the Key Players, but postpones other groups with high interest (branch operations, the data protection officer, logistics) to Phase B, even though the head pharmacists are already pointing to impacts and stakeholders need to be engaged in time. A questionnaire and the same information for everyone are a weak substitute for stakeholder analysis. Ignoring key groups until the vision is approved contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A Czech bank wants to launch fully digital account opening in a mobile app within a year. The CFO advocates extending the existing core banking and onboarding module, because it requires the smallest investment. The Chief Digital Officer wants a new cloud onboarding platform from a fintech supplier, which promises launch within six months. The CISO points to AML/KYC requirements, identity verification and outsourcing rules, and the back-office director mainly wants to eliminate manual document checks, which currently occupy forty people. Among the bank's architecture principles is “re-use before buy and buy before build”, and since last year also a goal of reducing the number of suppliers. The steering committee will meet in three weeks and has asked the lead architect to “choose the best architecture”. The work is in Phase A and the target vision has so far been formulated only in general terms.
question: How should the lead architect proceed according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: From the vision, principles, requirements and constraints, and from the concerns of all four stakeholders, derive criteria ranging from cost and time through risk and compliance to operational impact, identify alternatives and their combinations, and show their consequences in views for the individual stakeholders. Present the options to the steering committee for decision and record the decision with its justification so that it is traceable.

Derive criteria from the vision, principles and concerns of the CFO, the CDO and the back-office director, identify alternatives including combinations, and show their consequences in views. Present the options to the steering committee for decision; verify the CISO's AML/KYC and outsourcing requirements only after an option is selected, within a compliance review, so that they do not delay the decision.

Arrange individual meetings with all four managers, find out which option each prefers and why, and let the steering committee vote on the options, so that the decision has the widest possible support. The lead architect then elaborates the winning option into an Architecture Vision and Statement of Architecture Work and submits them to the steering committee for approval.

Select the fintech supplier's cloud platform, because it is the only one that promises launch within six months and best matches the digitalisation goal, and present it to the steering committee as a finished architecture recommendation (with detailed justification). Then incorporate the objections of the CFO and the CISO into negotiations with the supplier on price, contractual terms and responsibilities for regulatory compliance.
explanation: The Architecture Alternatives and Trade-Offs technique requires deriving criteria (from the vision, principles, requirements, constraints and concerns), identifying alternatives and showing their consequences – the architect makes the trade-offs visible, but stakeholders or the authorised body decide. The best answer does this for all stakeholders and documents the decision. The second option is methodologically correct, but omits the CISO's concerns, which can rule out any option, and addresses them too late. Voting by preference without an analysis of consequences is weak; selection of an option by the architect and setting aside the objections of key stakeholders contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A consumer credit company is finishing the architecture of a new loan approval process (Phases B and C). The lead architect has sent all stakeholders the complete ninety-page Architecture Definition Document with dozens of ArchiMate diagrams: to the board of directors, the heads of the approver teams, IT operations, the external supplier and internal audit. Board members did not read the document. The approvers complain that they cannot see how their day-to-day work will change and who will decide on exceptions. IT operations asks about responsibilities for running the new services, and internal audit wants to know how fraud controls and the audit trail will be ensured. The supplier is waiting for materials in order to estimate the effort, and the board is to decide on continuation immediately after the review. The formal stakeholder review is scheduled in two weeks.
question: What should the lead architect do according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: For each group, start from its concerns, choose viewpoints and create views that respond to those concerns: for the board the benefits and costs with a roadmap, for the approvers the impacts on processes and roles, for operations the responsibilities, for audit the controls and data flows. Keep the views consistent with the ADD, because they are views of the same architecture, and use them in the formal review.

For the board, prepare a view with benefits, costs and a roadmap, and for the approvers a view with impacts on processes and roles, because they are key players with the greatest influence. Leave IT operations, the supplier and internal audit with the complete ADD, because they are technically proficient and will find the details they need in it themselves, and conduct the review with them over the whole document.

Prepare a ten-page summary of the ADD with a glossary and simplified diagrams and send it to all stakeholder groups as a uniform basis for the review. Keep the complete ADD available in the repository for those who need the detail, so that everyone works from the same version of information and no contradictions in interpretation arise between the board, operations and audit.

Postpone the review and organise ArchiMate notation training for the board, approvers, operations, audit and the supplier, after which they will be able to find their way around the complete ADD themselves. One document for everyone ensures that nobody works with incomplete or differing information, and the training will also pay off in the company's further architecture projects.
explanation: According to TOGAF, the architect selects viewpoints according to the concerns of individual stakeholders and creates views that show how those concerns are addressed; one view can serve multiple stakeholders and all must be consistent with the ADD. The best answer does this for all groups including operations and audit. The second option tailors views for only some of the stakeholders and leaves the specific concerns of operations and audit unanswered. One summary for everyone is “the same view for everyone” and does not address concerns; notation training and one document for everyone negates the point of views.
