scenario: A brewing group with four breweries in the Czech Republic is automating its bottling plants and centralising distribution into a new logistics centre. The programme will affect roughly 400 employees in production and warehouses and is in Phase A. The finance director and the production director actively direct the programme and decide its key issues. A representative of the foreign parent company approves the investment within the group's investment plan, but is not interested in the programme's details. The trade unions representing the bottling plant employees are worried about jobs and follow the programme closely; they do not decide on the programme and cannot stop it, but they have the statutory right to be informed of organisational changes in good time and to discuss them. Packaging material suppliers will be affected by the change only marginally. In the draft Stakeholder Map, the lead architect put everyone into the same regime: a monthly newsletter on the programme status.
question: Which approach to stakeholder engagement is best according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Classify stakeholders by power and interest: manage both directors as Key Players with full involvement in decision-making, keep the parent company representative in Keep Satisfied mode with concise materials at milestones, the unions in Keep Informed mode with regular two-way communication about impacts, and merely monitor the packaging suppliers. Reflect all of this in the Stakeholder Map and Communications Plan.

Classify stakeholders by power and interest: manage both directors as Key Players, keep the parent company representative in Keep Satisfied mode and merely monitor the packaging suppliers. Put the unions into Minimal Effort mode, because they do not formally decide on the programme, and inform them only at implementation, when the impacts on jobs will be known; reflect all of this in the Stakeholder Map and Communications Plan.

Involve every group as intensively as Key Players: invite the parent company representative, the unions and the packaging suppliers to weekly architecture workshops and give them all working outputs for comment. Equal treatment of all stakeholders will prevent anyone feeling neglected and will increase overall trust in the programme and the architecture team.

Keep the uniform monthly newsletter for everyone, but actively work only with the parent company representative and the finance director, who decide on money, budget and the investment plan. The production director and the unions receive detailed information only after the investment is approved, so that resistance does not arise prematurely and complicate approval.
explanation: The power/interest grid in the Stakeholder Management technique determines the approach: high power and high interest = Key Players (full involvement), high power and low interest = Keep Satisfied, low power and high interest = Keep Informed, low power and low interest = Minimal Effort (monitor). The best answer thus classifies all groups and reflects the result in the Stakeholder Map and Communications Plan. The second option wrongly underestimates the unions, which have high interest and the right to be informed of changes in good time; the Minimal Effort mode and information only at implementation will provoke needless resistance. Equally intensive involvement of everyone wastes effort and burdens stakeholders with low interest; excluding a key player and informing them only after the decision contradicts TOGAF.

image.alt: Power/interest grid for Stakeholder Management with four quadrants: Keep Satisfied, Key Players, Minimal Effort and Keep Informed.

scenario: An automotive supplier with five plants in the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary wants to unify its manufacturing execution system (MES) and production data collection. According to the sponsor, the group's chief operating officer, the programme is to reduce system maintenance costs by a third and make it possible to compare line performance across plants. The directors of the two largest plants resist standardisation: they invested in local systems in the past, fear losing autonomy and cite the specifics of their lines. The director of the smaller Slovak plant, by contrast, welcomes standardisation. Without the support of both opponents the programme cannot be introduced in their plants, and one of them also has strong influence on the CEO. Architecture is in Phase A, the first version of the Architecture Vision is ready and the lead architect is deciding how to continue working with these stakeholders.
question: How should the lead architect proceed according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Classify the positions of both directors – the current and required level of understanding, commitment and support, and the ability to disrupt the programme – and manage them as Key Players. Engage them early directly in workshops, document their concerns, reflect legitimate specifics in the vision, show them views with benefits for the plants and, with the sponsor, plan how to close the gap in support.

Invite both directors to workshops, document their concerns and reflect legitimate plant specifics in the vision and principles, so that they identify with the result. Do not specifically assess the difference between their current and required support or the influence of one of them on the CEO, and do not plan the approach with the sponsor, because the workshops should dissipate the resistance on their own.

Ask the chief operating officer, as sponsor, to issue a binding instruction that all plants will move to the standard MES, and record the plant directors' objections as risks in the Statement of Architecture Work. Then regularly inform the plant directors about the results of the individual phases so that they know what awaits them and can prepare for the change in good time.

Remove both plants from the programme scope so that the conflict does not jeopardise the deadline, and carry out standardisation in the remaining three smaller plants. Adjust the scope straight away in the Architecture Vision and inform the sponsor of the change when the Statement of Architecture Work is submitted for approval, when the vision will already be finished and the change of scope justified in detail.
explanation: The Classify Stakeholder Positions step in the Stakeholder Management technique assesses the stakeholder's ability to disrupt the change and the gap between the current and required level of understanding, commitment and support; targeted engagement of key players and updating of the Stakeholder Map and Communications Plan are based on this. The best answer combines this with addressing concerns and involving the sponsor. The second option works well with concerns, but does not analyse the gap in support or the director's influence on the CEO, so the risk remains unmanaged. A directive instruction without addressing concerns is weak and merely shifts the resistance into implementation; one-sided narrowing of scope without the sponsor contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A ministry is preparing a new portal for submitting business permit applications, which will be used by approximately 200,000 entrepreneurs and by officials at fourteen regional offices. In workshops, stakeholders formulate “requirements” such as “the portal must be user-friendly”, “must be secure”, “must be modern” and “must be connected to everything”. The legal department points out that on 1 January 2028 a new law takes effect that changes the deadlines and supporting documents of applications. Between workshops, individual departments send their ideas by e-mail directly to the developers of the portal's existing supplier, who has already started implementing some of them. The lead architect is to prepare, from the results, the basis for the Architecture Requirements Specification while maintaining the trust of stakeholders, who complain that their suggestions were lost in the past.
question: How should the lead architect manage stakeholder engagement and their requirements according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Treat the wishes as concerns and with stakeholders derive from them unambiguous, testable requirements tied to objectives; record the law's effective date as a constraint. Introduce a single channel so that suggestions are not lost. Record requirements in the requirements repository, manage changes in Requirements Management with an impact assessment, and show stakeholders how their concerns are reflected in the design.

Treat the wishes as concerns and with stakeholders convert them into measurable and testable requirements tied to objectives, record the law's effective date as a constraint and record everything in the requirements repository. However, leave the departments the option of submitting minor modifications directly to the supplier, so that speed and responsiveness to the business are not lost, and add them to the repository retrospectively according to the supplier's reports.

Take the wording from the workshops literally into the Architecture Requirements Specification, so that stakeholders recognise their requirements, and have all departments sign the document. The signature will secure their commitment and, if needed, new requirements will be added to the next version of the document, which all affected departments will again sign, thereby confirming its completeness.

Ask the existing supplier to propose the shape of the new portal according to the features of its product, and derive the requirements from its proposal. Stakeholders will thus see a concrete solution and stop formulating vague wishes, the supplier will be able to continue the modifications it has already started for the departments, and the law's effective date will be easier to meet.
explanation: A concern is a stakeholder's interest, whereas a requirement must be unambiguous and testable or measurable; the architect should refine concerns with stakeholders, tie them to objectives and constraints, and manage requirements in one repository, with changes governed by Requirements Management with an impact assessment. The best answer also stops the parallel channel directly to the supplier, which bypasses requirements management. The second option refines requirements correctly, but leaves this channel in place, so the record will not be complete. Taking vague wishes literally into the ARS does not make them testable requirements; deriving requirements from the supplier's product is a classic “solution looking for a problem”.

scenario: A pension company manages the savings of approximately 900,000 clients and its infrastructure runs in two of its own data centres, whose hardware is at the end of its life. The company therefore plans to move the client portal and the document archive to the public cloud; the provider offers data centres in several EU countries. For such a significant outsourcing, the supervisory authority (the Czech National Bank) will want evidence of data location, an exit strategy, assurance of operational continuity and supplier risk management. The CEO mainly follows savings, the data protection officer deals with the processing of clients' personal data and internal audit asks for demonstrable controls. Architecture is in Phases B and C and the target state is only now taking shape. The lead architect wanted to send the regulator the same presentation as they prepared for the board – benefits, costs and schedule.
question: How should the lead architect take the regulator into account according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Include the regulator among the key external stakeholders and reflect its concerns about data location and exit strategy, continuity and supplier risk in the requirements in the ARS straight away, because the target is only taking shape. For these concerns choose viewpoints and create views consistent with the ADD, verify them with compliance, the data protection officer and audit, and include the communication in the Communications Plan.

For the regulator, create separate views showing data location, exit strategy, continuity and supplier risk management, and verify the content with compliance, the data protection officer and internal audit. Prepare the views only after the target architecture is finished and approved, so that the regulator receives a final and stable version and does not have to be presented with interim design changes or unfinished options.

Send the regulator the complete Architecture Definition Document supplemented with the cloud provider's certifications (e.g. ISO 27001 and SOC 2), because it contains all the details of the target solution. Any follow-up questions from the regulator will then be answered by the lead architect together with the cloud service supplier, who knows the technical details of the solution.

Do not include the regulator in the architecture work; the outsourcing notification will be submitted by the legal department only before the portal is launched. Architecture will focus on internal stakeholders and on the savings the CEO requires, because communication with the supervisory authority is not the task of architects but of the compliance and legal units, who have it in their job description.
explanation: The regulator is an external stakeholder with high power; its concerns need to be identified early, reflected in the requirements, and viewpoints chosen for them, from which views arise showing how the architecture addresses the concerns. The best answer does this during the development of the architecture, so the concerns can influence the target state, and includes communication in the Communications Plan. The second option uses the right technique, but too late – the regulator's concerns then cannot influence the design and rework is likely. Sending the whole ADD with the supplier's certifications is not a view focused on concerns; leaving out the regulator entirely contradicts stakeholder management.

image.alt: Relationships between the terms stakeholder, concern, viewpoint and view: a stakeholder has concerns, a viewpoint frames them and governs views, and a view addresses concerns.

scenario: A large Czech university with nine faculties is starting a programme to unify its student information system, e-learning and research data management. The sponsor is the rector, the budget was approved by the board of trustees and part of the funding has a fixed drawdown deadline. The faculties have high autonomy, the deans protect their own systems, and both students and academics are sceptical of IT changes. A previous attempt at unification five years ago failed, among other reasons, because the faculties learned about the planned changes from unofficial sources and felt that decisions were being made about them without them. The programme is in Phase A, the Stakeholder Map is finished and the lead architect is preparing the Communications Plan; the academic senate will give its opinion on the programme in two months.
question: Which Communications Plan best corresponds to the TOGAF Standard and the university's situation?
options: Start from the Stakeholder Map and group stakeholders by communication needs into management and deans, the academic senate, academics and students, IT and suppliers. For each group determine key messages and channels, responsibilities and a schedule tied to ADM milestones, feedback and risks. Communicate in good time and regularly from the start of Phase A, and update the plan continuously.

Start from the Stakeholder Map and group stakeholders by communication needs (management, deans, academic senate, academics, students, IT, suppliers). For each group determine key messages, channels, responsibilities and the means of feedback. However, begin communication towards the faculties only after the Architecture Vision is approved, so that unverified information does not spread among academics.

Prepare a uniform monthly newsletter on the programme status and, from the approval of the Architecture Vision, send it to all university employees and students, together with a programme web page with all documents and a contact form. Uniform communication ensures that everyone receives the same, already verified information at the same time.

Entrust communication with stakeholders to the external relations (PR) department, which will start it after the implementation is complete, when there will be something to show, and let the architecture team concentrate on design. The deans will be informed about the programme's progress by the rector at the collegium as needed, because communication with the faculties is their responsibility, not a task for architects.
explanation: The Communications Plan is an output of Phase A and is based on the Stakeholder Map: it groups stakeholders by communication needs and determines key messages, mechanisms, responsibilities, a schedule and risks; the benefit of stakeholder management is to communicate in good time and often. The best answer contains all of this and begins communicating immediately, which directly addresses the cause of the previous failure. The second option has the right structure of the plan, but postponing communication with the faculties until the vision is approved repeats the mistake for which the previous attempt failed. A uniform newsletter, moreover sent only from the approval of the vision, does not distinguish the needs of groups and postpones communication for everyone, not just the faculties; entrusting communication to the PR department only after implementation contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: The enterprise architecture team of a telecommunications operator (twelve architects) is working in parallel on the modernisation of the 5G core, the consolidation of billing and a new B2B portal. Each architect creates their own types of diagrams and presentations. The Architecture Board decides, among other things, on shared network and IT platforms, the options for which are submitted by various projects, and its members complain that every document looks different and the options cannot be compared. Recurring stakeholder groups – network operations, security, product managers and finance – receive inconsistent views of the same things from different projects and sometimes even answers to questions they did not ask. The new CTO wants the Board to decide faster and on the basis of comparable materials. The company uses a modelling tool with ArchiMate support.
question: What should the lead architect introduce according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Build in the Reference Library a library of viewpoints for recurring classes of stakeholders, including the Architecture Board, and their concerns – with purpose, audience, model kinds and conventions – so that the materials are comparable. In each project, then determine the key stakeholders and their concerns, select viewpoints from the library, supplementing new ones where necessary, and create views according to them.

Build in the Reference Library a library of viewpoints for recurring classes of stakeholders and their concerns with purpose, audience, model kinds and conventions, and introduce uniform viewpoints for decision-making for the Board. Each project would, however, be obliged to create views according to all viewpoints from the library, regardless of which stakeholders and concerns are relevant in the given project.

Issue a binding graphic style guide for diagrams in ArchiMate notation (colours, layout, legends, presentation templates) and require its observance in all projects and in materials for the Board. A uniform appearance of materials will allow the Architecture Board and other stakeholders to read materials from different projects easily, compare them with each other and decide on them faster.

Stop creating separate views for individual stakeholders and publish the complete enterprise model in the tool's portal, where every stakeholder, including Board members, can find and filter what interests them. This eliminates inconsistency between materials, because everyone will work with the same, always up-to-date model, and architects will save the time spent preparing presentations.
explanation: When creating views, TOGAF recommends first using an existing library of viewpoints (part of the Reference Library), determining the key stakeholders, analysing their concerns, selecting viewpoints and creating views according to them – the library ensures reusability and consistency, including for the Architecture Board as one of the classes of stakeholders. The best answer combines the library with selection according to the concerns of the specific project. The second option has a library, but enforces all views regardless of relevant concerns, which leads to unnecessary work. A style guide unifies appearance, but not content focused on concerns; leaving stakeholders to find their way around the whole model negates the architect's role of creating views for their concerns.

image.alt: Relationships between the terms stakeholder, concern, viewpoint and view: a stakeholder has concerns, a viewpoint frames them and governs views, and a view addresses concerns.

scenario: A regional integrated transport organiser has received from the regional council a Request for Architecture Work for a unified ticketing and passenger information system for buses, trains and urban transport in three statutory cities. The sponsor is the deputy governor for transport. A three-person architecture team began working informally: it runs workshops with carriers and draws target diagrams in a modelling tool. Nobody has yet clarified how the work ties into the region's project and portfolio management, who will approve the outputs, what resources and budget the architecture work has available, or how the cities, which operate their own transport companies, will take part in it. The region has had an Architecture Board and a tailored framework for architecture work since last year. In fourteen months regional elections are held and the deputy governor wants visible results by then.
question: What should the lead architect do now according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Formally establish the architecture project: in accordance with the Tailored Architecture Framework and the region's project management, confirm the sponsor and the Architecture Board as the approving body and determine roles, resources and a plan. Only then continue with the steps of Phase A – stakeholders and concerns of carriers, cities and passengers, objectives, drivers and constraints including the elections, scope and vision – and conclude with the SoAW for approval.

Continue with workshops with carriers and the creation of the vision, because the pressure for results is great, and clarify the link to the region's project management, approving bodies, roles, resources and budget only when writing the Statement of Architecture Work at the end of Phase A. Before its approval, then add the missing stakeholders, in particular the cities with their own transport companies and passenger representatives.

Compile a detailed schedule of all phases (A to H) with fixed deadlines tied to the elections and, in parallel with Phase A, start modelling in Phases B and C to save time. Resolve governance and approval of outputs on an ongoing basis directly with the deputy governor as needed, because the Architecture Board meets only four times a year and could delay the work.

By a quick market survey select the ticketing system supplier, so that concrete results are visible by the elections, and tailor the architecture to its solution. Then use the workshops with carriers and cities to agree on the selected product, price list and schedule, and to prepare a pilot deployment on the routes most visible to passengers and the media.
explanation: The first step of Phase A is Establish the Architecture Project – ensuring that the architecture work has a framework in the enterprise's project and portfolio management, a confirmed sponsor, governance, roles and resources according to the Tailored Architecture Framework; this is followed by the identification of stakeholders, objectives and constraints, scope, vision and approval of the SoAW. The best answer follows this order and takes into account the specific stakeholders and the election deadline. The second option leads to the same outputs, but postpones establishing the project to the end, so the work runs without a mandate and rework is likely. Starting Phases B and C in parallel without approval and “as needed” governance is weak; selecting a product before the vision contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A dairy group has taken over a competitor and the CEO has issued a Request for Architecture Work for “integrated supply chain planning” from the purchase of milk from farmers to distribution to retail chains. Key information is, however, missing: the board will decide on the target operating model (centralised or regional planning) only in three months, there is only incomplete data on the systems of the acquired company because its IT was managed by an external supplier, and the budget for integration is approved only for the first year. The acquired company has its own planning team and a different way of procuring milk from farmers, and the integration is managed by a committee composed of directors of both companies. The retail chains are meanwhile pressing for more accurate deliveries and product freshness. The sponsor wants the Architecture Vision within six weeks so that they can use it as a basis for the board's decision on the operating model.
question: How should the lead architect deal with the missing information in Phase A according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Determine what information the vision needs, gather what is available and replace the missing information with explicit assumptions and open questions. Develop the vision at the level of detail needed for the decision and with alternatives of the centralised and regional model, including their benefits and risks, so that the board has something to choose from. In the SoAW plan further iterations to refine the architecture after the decision.

Determine what information the vision needs, gather what is available and replace the missing information with explicit assumptions. Build the vision on the most likely centralised model, because one clear vision is easier to present to the board than several options, document the assumption and in the Statement of Architecture Work plan refinement in the next iteration.

Pause Phase A until the board decides on the operating model and until a complete inventory of the acquired company's systems is available. In the meantime carry out a detailed inventory of the applications, interfaces and data flows of both companies, so that the vision rests on complete and verified data and does not need to be reworked later; explain to the sponsor that the six-week deadline for the vision is not realistic under these circumstances.

Skip the vision and start Phases B and C straight away with detailed modelling of the current state of both companies; write the vision retrospectively from the results of the modelling. The board will thus receive materials built on facts, not assumptions, and architects will gain a head start for later phases and for the integration of the acquired company's systems, which will have to be carried out in any case.
explanation: The ADM is iterative: in each iteration the scope and level of detail are chosen as needed and missing information is filled in in later iterations, with assumptions explicitly documented. The best answer also prepares alternatives, because the vision is to serve precisely as a basis for the board's decision. The second option uses iteration correctly, but prematurely commits to one option and offers the board no choice. Pausing Phase A and waiting for complete data negates the iterative approach; skipping the vision and starting with detailed modelling contradicts the ADM.

scenario: A statutory city with 300,000 inhabitants has issued a Request for Architecture Work for a “digital architecture of the city”. The mayor wants to cover everything within nine months: transport and parking, waste management, energy in municipal buildings, electronic submissions, education and social services. They want to show results to citizens as soon as possible, but the architecture team has only four people and a limited budget. In ten months a European funds call closes, to which the city wants to submit smart parking and electronic submissions projects; the applications will need to evidence a target architecture and a link to the national eGovernment architecture. The city council will vote on the projects in eight months. Some municipal organisations (the transport company, technical services) have their own IT and their own plans, and the IT department has kept a several-years-old inventory of the city's applications.
question: How should the lead architect define the scope in Phase A according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: With the sponsor, define the scope in all dimensions: breadth, with areas and organisations ranked by value and by the call deadline; the depth needed for the vision and the applications; a time horizon with intermediate states; and the domains affected. Determine partitions with respect to organisations with their own IT and assets to be reused, such as the national architecture and the application inventory, take the team's capacity into account and record the scope in the SoAW.

With the sponsor, limit the breadth to smart parking and electronic submissions because of the call deadline and plan the other areas for later cycles. For both areas, however, develop all four domains down to the physical level of detail, so that the applications contain complete technical documentation including specific technologies, and record the scope in the Statement of Architecture Work.

Accept the mayor's scope in its full breadth and reconcile it with the team's capacity by producing for all areas (from transport to social services) only a very general overview without prioritisation. At the same time, ask for the team to be strengthened with further architects, so that all areas can be developed within nine months with comparable quality and depth and none is disadvantaged.

Let each department and municipal organisation determine the scope and architecture of its own area according to its needs, and merge the results after nine months into one city architecture. The architecture team will collect, unify and formally check the submitted materials, without interfering in the competences of departments and organisations with their own IT.
explanation: When defining scope in Phase A, the breadth, depth, time horizon and architecture domains are determined, as well as partitions and assets to be reused; scope is limited according to resources, competences and real value, and the rest is addressed in further cycles. The best answer works with all dimensions and with priority according to the call deadline, and records the result in the SoAW. The second option rightly narrows breadth, but ignores the dimension of depth – physical detail in Phase A is unnecessary and the team will not manage it. Full breadth with superficial detail brings no value for the call; leaving architecture to individual departments contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A water utility supplying 400,000 inhabitants has received from the CEO a Request for Architecture Work with a single sentence: “Introduce smart water meters.” Interviews reveal more. The CFO wants to reduce water losses in the network (non-revenue water) by a third within five years, the cities as owners demand a stable water price, operations want to reduce manual meter reading and customer service wants to report leaks to customers in good time. The subsidy on which the company relies requires completion by the end of 2028 and household consumption data are subject to personal data protection. The goals of finance and the owners partly conflict, because investments will be reflected in the price of water. The CEO will present the result to the general assembly of municipalities, and operations point out that part of the network lies in difficult terrain. Architecture is at the beginning of Phase A.
question: Which approach is most appropriate for the lead architect according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Confirm and elaborate the business goals, drivers and constraints: uncover the real drivers of the technology brief in the form of water losses, costs and customer services, turn the goals into measurable SMART objectives and record the constraints arising from the subsidy, personal data protection and the budget. Resolve the conflict between investment and a stable price with the sponsor and owners before defining the scope.

Confirm and elaborate the business goals, drivers and constraints: uncover the real drivers behind the brief, turn the goals into measurable SMART objectives and record the constraints (subsidy deadline, personal data protection, budget). Document the conflict between investment and a stable water price and leave its resolution to Phase B, when the details of the design and the costs will be known.

Take over the brief “introduce smart water meters” as the main objective, document the technical constraints (radio band, battery life, network coverage) and measure success by the share of meters installed. Record the other stakeholder wishes as supplementary requirements for later phases, which will not extend the scope that the CEO clearly and unambiguously specified.

Because of the subsidy deadline, immediately issue a tender for a smart meter supplier and derive the architecture's objectives from its case studies and references from other water utilities. Conflicts between stakeholders will be resolved once it is clear what the selected solution can do, and architecture will then describe its deployment so that it is possible to demonstrate to the subsidy provider that all of its conditions are met.
explanation: The Phase A step Confirm and Elaborate Business Goals, Business Drivers, and Constraints is meant to uncover the real business reasons for the change, express goals measurably and capture constraints; conflicts between goals must be resolved with the sponsor before the scope and vision are defined. The best answer does this completely. The second option is methodologically correct, but postpones the key conflict of goals to Phase B, where it can no longer be resolved well and jeopardises approval of the vision. Taking over the technology as the goal and measuring success by the number of meters confuses the solution with the goal; a tender before the vision contradicts the ADM.

scenario: A state office paying out social benefits (3,000 case officers at branches) wants to digitise the processing of applications. Two previous attempts failed – one because of a lack of internal IT capacity, the other after a change of leadership, when the new director stopped supporting the project. Case officers work mostly with paper forms and their unions fear that digitisation will lead to redundancies. The internal IT has twenty people and is heavily dependent on external suppliers, and public procurement takes over a year. Branch directors have great autonomy in organising work and the ministry, as founder, requires quarterly reporting on the progress of large projects. The office has funding secured from European funds for the first two years. The new Director General has issued a Request for Architecture Work and wants digitisation within three years. Architecture is in Phase A.
question: How should the lead architect approach the organisation's readiness for change according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Carry out a Business Transformation Readiness Assessment in cross-functional workshops with management and branches, IT and procurement: determine all factors including vision and willingness, sponsorship and funding, governance and the capacity of IT and units, assess the urgency, status and difficulty of remediation for each and propose measures. Include the results in the Capability Assessment and reflect them in scope and risks.

Carry out a Business Transformation Readiness Assessment focused on IT: the capacities of internal IT, skills, dependence on suppliers and the length of public procurement; assess the urgency, status and difficulty of remediation for each factor and propose measures. Include the results in the Capability Assessment and reflect them in scope, risks and approach in the vision and SoAW.

Record the low readiness as a risk in the Statement of Architecture Work and include extensive training of case officers in Phase G in the plan, so that they are prepared for the new system in time. The organisation's readiness will be assessed in more detail only in Phase E, when specific solutions and suppliers will be known and the real difficulty of the change can be estimated (from branches through unions to suppliers and internal IT).

Do not address readiness, because the new Director General clearly supports the programme and the past failures were caused by different people in a different situation. Build the vision on digitising all agendas, forms and branches within three years, so that the programme has sufficient ambition, motivates employees to change quickly and can obtain funding from European funds.
explanation: The Business Transformation Readiness Assessment is first carried out in Phase A (the step Assess Readiness for Business Transformation), typically in the form of cross-functional workshops; factors are rated by urgency, state of readiness and difficulty of remediation, and the results are part of the Capability Assessment and influence scope and risks. The best answer covers all relevant factors including sponsorship, which caused one of the failures. The second option proceeds technically correctly, but limits itself to IT and omits the units and management. Merely recording a risk and postponing the assessment to Phase E is weak; ignoring readiness after two failures contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A network of private clinics is preparing a telemedicine platform: video consultations with doctors, sharing of medical records with patients and integration with laboratories. The platform will be used by doctors at 25 clinics and approximately 150,000 registered patients. Patients will use the platform mainly from a mobile app, the clinics have different outpatient systems and the laboratories are external partners. It involves health data, which is a special category of personal data. Management wants to launch the platform by the end of next year, because competitors already offer a similar service. Architecture is in Phase A. The CISO insists that the vision cannot be approved until a detailed security architecture with all measures, encryption algorithms and network zones is finished. The sales director as sponsor, by contrast, claims that security is a technical detail for later phases and wants to submit the vision for approval within a month.
question: How should the lead architect address security in Phase A according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Do a “sufficient” security design in Phase A: with the CISO and sponsor confirm the security principles, risk appetite and regulatory constraints and identify the main risks of the vision with high-level mitigation. The CISO thus gains assurance that no unknown or unacceptable risks remain, and the sponsor that security will enable the benefits at a reasonable price; leave the detailed design to Phases B–D.

Record in the vision and the SoAW the security principles, regulatory constraints for health data and the main security risks with high-level mitigation. Involve the CISO in the work from Phase B, when detailed design begins, so that their requirements do not delay approval of the vision that the sponsor is seeking, and then incorporate their comments into the Architecture Requirements Specification.

Accommodate the CISO and, before approval of the vision, produce a detailed security architecture with all measures, encryption algorithms and network zones. Approval of the vision will be pushed back by several months, but security will be resolved in detail from the outset, the CISO will be satisfied and later phases will no longer have to deal with it in detail.

Accommodate the sponsor: do not address security in Phase A and submit the vision for approval without it, because it is a technical detail. Security measures will be designed in Phase D together with the technology architecture, when the specific platform will be known, and their effectiveness will be verified by penetration tests before going live and evidenced by the platform provider's certification and an independent audit.
explanation: According to G152, Phase A should contain only as much security-specific design as is needed for security stakeholders to be assured that the target state has no unknown or unacceptable risks and conforms to policies, and for the business and budget owners to see that security will enable the benefits with the right balance of risk, compliance and benefit. The best answer does precisely this “sufficient” level and involves both stakeholders. The second option has the right content but excludes the CISO, whose assurance is the condition of sufficiency. A detailed security architecture in Phase A is detail in the wrong phase; omitting security and adding it later in Phase D contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A freight forwarding and logistics company is preparing a “control tower” – real-time visibility of shipments across carriers, warehouses and customs processes; according to the business strategy it is to be the company's main competitive advantage in large customers' tenders. The company has 1,200 employees and branches in five countries, and data will be shared with carriers and customers. After five weeks of Phase A, the lead architect has a Stakeholder Map, a draft vision with several diagrams and a list of risks. The chief operating officer as sponsor has declared: “The vision is clear, we start Phase B tomorrow; the Statement of Architecture Work is just bureaucracy.” The Architecture Board meets in two weeks. The data sharing requirements of two key customers are not yet confirmed and the IT director does not yet agree on how many people to release for the architecture work.
question: What should the lead architect do according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Explain to the sponsor that the SoAW, as an agreement on scope and approach, roles, plan and acceptance criteria, protects them too. Before the Board meeting, finish the Architecture Vision with key requirements and KPIs, the SoAW and the Communications Plan, confirm the customers' requirements and agree resources with the IT director; start Phase B only after approval by the sponsor and the Board.

Explain to the sponsor that the SoAW is an agreement on scope, approach, roles, plan and acceptance criteria. Before the Board meeting, finish the Architecture Vision and the SoAW and have them approved by the sponsor and the Architecture Board; settle the Communications Plan and the agreement with customers and with the IT director on resources during Phase B, so as not to delay approval.

Accommodate the sponsor and start Phase B immediately, because the vision is clear enough and time matters. Complete the Statement of Architecture Work in parallel during Phase B and have it approved by the sponsor and the Board afterwards, once the details are known (scope, resources from the IT director, the requirements of the two key customers), because without them the SoAW would not be complete anyway.

Skip the vision and the SoAW and approach three or four control tower solution suppliers straight away to demonstrate their products on the data of the company, carriers and customs processes; derive the architecture from the selected solution. Feasibility, price and benefit for tenders will be shown fastest, and the sponsor and key customers will see a concrete result.
explanation: Phase A ends with approval of the Statement of Architecture Work by the sponsor (and by governance, e.g. the Architecture Board); together with the Architecture Vision and the Communications Plan, these are the outputs needed to begin further phases. The SoAW serves as an agreement on scope, roles, plan and acceptance criteria, so the best answer completes all three outputs, closes open points with customers and IT, and only then moves to Phase B. The second option obtains approval, but without the Communications Plan and without confirmed resources and requirements, which jeopardises further work. Starting Phase B before approval is the wrong order; skipping the vision and starting with products contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A regional rail operator running 120 electric and diesel multiple units wants to introduce predictive maintenance: sensors on vehicles, data collection and its analysis. Maintenance is currently planned according to kilometres travelled and fixed intervals. Architecture is in Phase A and the draft vision so far contains only technology diagrams – sensors, a data lake and an analytics platform. The CFO stated in the steering committee that she will not support further funding until it is clear what value the target architecture will bring and by what measure success will be judged. The operations director is interested in the number of cancelled services, and the region, as the transport authority, in penalties for failing to keep to the timetable; it is also negotiating a new ten-year public service obligation contract with the operator and wants to see how the operator will improve reliability.
question: How should the lead architect supplement the vision according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Define the value propositions of the target architecture for individual stakeholders (fewer cancelled services and penalties, lower maintenance costs, higher vehicle availability) and tie them to business goals and drivers. For each, set a measurable KPI with a baseline and target value, agree them directly with the CFO, operations and the region, and reflect them in the vision and SoAW.

Define the value propositions of the target architecture (fewer cancelled services and penalties, lower maintenance costs, higher vehicle availability) and measurable KPIs with target values taken from industry benchmarks. Submit the vision with them to the steering committee, without verifying the KPIs with operations and the region and without establishing their baseline values in today's operations.

Add to the vision technical KPIs of the target solution, such as the availability of the analytics platform, the latency of data transmission from sensors, the accuracy of prediction models and the number of units equipped, because these can be measured from the moment of launch. The benefits for operations and finance will be quantified only after introduction, when actual operational data will be available and can be reliably compared with the current state.

Explain to the CFO that value will show only in operation, and instead of elaborating the vision start a pilot installation (sensors, data lake and analytics) on a few units. The pilot results will then serve as more convincing evidence for further funding, for the region and for the negotiations on the new contract, because they are based on real data from the company's own vehicles.
explanation: The Phase A step Define the Target Architecture Value Propositions and KPIs requires describing the value of the target architecture for stakeholders and setting measurable indicators by which success will be judged; this is exactly the CFO's concern. The best answer ties the propositions to goals and agrees the KPIs with the stakeholders concerned, including baseline values. The second option has the right structure, but without verification and baseline values the KPIs are neither credible nor practically measurable. Technical KPIs say nothing about business value; a pilot instead of a vision skips Phase A.

scenario: An online electronics retailer wants to launch a marketplace for external sellers within a year. The sponsor is the sales director, who promised shareholders a launch within twelve months. The company has 600 employees and an e-shop with 1.5 million active customers; competitors already run a marketplace and offer a many times larger range. The workshops on the vision are full of enthusiasm, but nobody has yet examined whether the company has the necessary capabilities: recruiting and managing sellers, settlement and payouts to partners, resolving disputes between customers and sellers, and managing a catalogue from third parties. IT has only limited experience with multi-tenant platforms and the architecture practice in the company is only now emerging. The CFO is worried about customer support costs in disputes. The repository contains a business capability map from last year's strategic cycle.
question: What should the lead architect do in Phase A according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Carry out the Evaluate Capabilities step, because without it the feasibility of the vision cannot be assessed: using the capability map from the repository, assess the current and target business, IT and architecture capabilities for the marketplace and identify gaps. Record the result in the Capability Assessment, discuss it with the sponsor and reflect it in scope, risks and the choice between in-house development, purchase and partnership.

Carry out the Evaluate Capabilities step focused on IT: assess experience with multi-tenant platforms, operational maturity and team capacities, and identify gaps. Record the result in the Capability Assessment, discuss it with the sponsor and reflect it in scope and risks in the vision and SoAW; assess the marketplace's business capabilities (seller recruitment, settlement, dispute resolution) in more detail only in Phase B.

Do not address capabilities in Phase A and concentrate on an attractive vision for the sponsor and shareholders; the necessary capabilities will emerge in Phase B during detailed modelling of the processes of seller recruitment, settlement and dispute resolution. Use the capability map from the repository only there, as a starting point for modelling the target state and estimating support costs.

Acquire a ready-made marketplace platform that “contains” the necessary capabilities, including seller recruitment, settlement, dispute resolution and catalogue management, and build the vision on its functions. Assessing the company's own capabilities thus becomes unnecessary, because the supplier takes over processes and operations, and the company can concentrate on marketing, acquiring sellers and fulfilling the promise to shareholders.
explanation: The Phase A step Evaluate Capabilities assesses current and target capabilities – business, IT and architecture – and the result is recorded in the Capability Assessment, which influences scope, risks and approach. The best answer uses the existing capability map and covers business and IT capabilities. The second option proceeds correctly, but limits itself to IT, even though the main gaps (seller management, settlement, disputes) are business ones. Postponing the assessment to Phase B means approving the vision without knowing feasibility; relying on a product to replace the company's own capabilities contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: An international airport that handles several million passengers a year, and whose airlines are pressing for shorter processing times, is preparing biometric processing and analytics of passenger flows. The Architecture Principles approved by the Architecture Board in the Preliminary Phase include, among others, the principles “Passenger data is stored in data centres in the Czech Republic”, “Buy before build” and “Single source of truth”. The draft vision counts on a global SaaS platform for biometrics that stores data in data centres in the EU but outside the Czech Republic; according to the sales director it is the only solution capable of meeting the start date of the summer season. Biometric data is a special category of personal data and the data protection officer has not yet been approached. The Architecture Board meets in three weeks and architecture is in Phase A.
question: How should the lead architect deal with the principles in Phase A according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Verify whether the existing principles apply to this initiative and analyse the conflict using their rationale and implications. Involve the data protection officer because of the biometric data and prepare as alternatives either compliance with the principle through a different solution, or a formal change of the principle if its rationale has changed. Leave the decision to the Architecture Board, because it approved the principles.

Verify whether the existing principles apply to this initiative and analyse the conflict using their rationale and implications. Prepare alternatives (compliance with the principle through a different solution, or a formal change of the principle if its rationale has changed) and submit the decision to the Architecture Board; involve the data protection officer from Phase C during the design of the data architecture, where personal data is addressed in detail.

Because principles are lasting and change only exceptionally, reject outright the vision built on the SaaS platform and limit it to solutions operated in the Czech Republic, regardless of the season's deadline. There is no need to examine alternatives or the impacts on the business case, because the principle is unambiguous, approved by the Architecture Board and compliance with it is binding for the airport.

Treat principles as general recommendations and proceed with the vision using the SaaS platform, because only it will meet the summer season deadline and corresponds to the principle “Buy before build”. The principles can be adjusted retrospectively to match the adopted solution, once the system is in operation and it is clear how it has proved itself; inform the data protection officer before launch.
explanation: Principles are established in the Preliminary Phase and confirmed and elaborated in Phase A; in a conflict, their rationale and implications are used, and principles are changed only through a formal process via governance. The best answer therefore analyses the conflict, prepares alternatives, involves the data protection officer because of the special category of data and leaves the decision to the Architecture Board. The second option has the right procedure, but involves the key stakeholder for biometric data too late. Mechanical rejection without alternatives ignores the business need and the possibility of a controlled change; retrospectively adapting principles to a finished solution contradicts governance.

scenario: A building society (900 employees) has an approved Statement of Architecture Work and Architecture Vision for “digital loan origination”: the client submits an application online, scoring runs automatically and the client receives a decision within 24 hours instead of today's ten days. Loans make up most of the society's revenue and the project's results will be assessed by the Architecture Board. Phase B begins. The repository contains a business capability map and process models from 2019, and the bank can use an industry reference model for lending processes. The segment architecture “Retail Lending”, approved last year, specifies shared services for client identification and document management, which other products already use. The business architect proposes first modelling in detail all 140 of the bank's current processes and only then dealing with the target state; the product owner, by contrast, wants to see the new processes as soon as possible.
question: How should the team proceed in Phase B according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Select the industry model and the capability map as reference models, viewpoints and tools according to stakeholders' concerns, describe the baseline only to the extent needed for the lending process and design the target state. Perform gap analysis and define candidate roadmap components, resolve the impacts on the shared identification and document services from the segment architecture, carry out a formal review and update the ADD and ARS.

Select reference models (the industry model, the capability map), viewpoints and tools, describe the baseline only to the extent needed for the lending process and design the target state. Perform gap analysis, define candidate roadmap components, carry out a formal review and update the ADD and ARS; design client identification and document management directly for the needs of the lending process.

First model in detail all 140 of the bank's current processes, so that the baseline is complete and nothing is overlooked, and only then design the target state, perform gap analysis and define candidate roadmap components. Carry out the formal review with stakeholders and the update of the ADD after both models are finished, so that stakeholders see the whole picture at once.

Select the lending software with the best automatic scoring and adopt its standard processes as the target Business Architecture, because they correspond to proven market practice and will significantly shorten Phase B. Then perform gap analysis between the current processes and the product's processes and resolve differences by adapting the bank's processes, not by costly and risky modification of the product.
explanation: Phase B goes through the common steps: selecting reference models, viewpoints and tools, baseline (only to the extent needed), target, gap analysis, candidate roadmap components, resolving impacts across the Architecture Landscape, formal stakeholder review, finalisation and updating the ADD. The best answer follows them and respects the superior segment architecture. The second option omits resolving impacts and designs its own identification and document management in conflict with the segment architecture. A complete detailed baseline of all processes is unnecessary effort; adopting the product's processes as the target Business Architecture means selecting a solution in Phase B, which contradicts the ADM.

scenario: A statutory city is digitising building permit proceedings at its building authority, which handles around 6,000 applications a year. The approved vision sets the goals: shorten the processing of an application from 90 to 30 days, reduce the number of decisions that the regional office overturns on appeal because of formal errors, and ensure compliance with the new building legislation and with the national builder's portal. The business principles include “data only once” and “digital by default”. Data on land plots and buildings is held by the land registry, which offers an interface for taking it over. The business architect delivered an elegant model of target processes. It nevertheless still requires applicants to re-enter data on plots from the land registry, and no part of it addresses how the error rate of decisions will be reduced. The formal review with stakeholders is in three weeks and the head of the building authority wants it to go without complications.
question: What should the lead architect do according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Before the review, verify the target Business Architecture against the goals, drivers and principles from Phase A, because it is supposed to be based on them: for each goal show how it will be measurably met, and, according to the principle “data only once”, design the takeover of plot data from the land registry with interoperability requirements. Fill the gaps, record the requirements in the ARS and refine the goals as needed.

Before the review, correct the conflict with the principle “data only once”: design the takeover of plot data from the land registry, including interoperability requirements, and record them in the ARS. Leave the reduction of decision error rate to Phase G, where the quality of processing will be verified by testing and compliance checks, and then carry out the review with stakeholders according to the original plan.

Submit the model for formal review as it is, because it is professionally of good quality and stakeholders can comment on it, and let them express themselves on the goals and principles. Capture any inconsistencies with the goals as Change Requests and resolve them in Phase H in the next cycle, so as not to delay the project schedule and so that the head of the building authority does not have to move the deadlines promised to the city council.

Ask the IT department to design the data model, application and integrations for processing applications now, according to the process model, and evaluate the goals of the vision after the system goes live, on real data. The Business Architecture will thus turn faster into a concrete solution that can be shown to builders, the city council and the regional office.
explanation: The business principles, goals and drivers from Phase A are a key input of Phases B–D: the target architecture must show how it meets the goals and how it respects the principles, and refine them as needed. The best answer ensures traceability of all goals (including the decision error rate) and principles and records the results in the ARS before the formal review. The second option addresses the principle “data only once”, but postpones the goal of reducing errors to Phase G, where one can only test, not design. Submitting an inconsistent model and resolving it only in Phase H is weak; designing an application and evaluating goals only after go-live contradicts the ADM.

scenario: A telecommunications operator wants to launch an offering of IoT connectivity and managed services for corporate customers within 18 months. The operator has 2,000 employees, corporate customers make up a quarter of its revenue and competitors already offer similar services. The vision is approved and Phase B begins. Business stakeholders cannot agree which units and partners the change affects: product managers talk about products, sales about the customer journey, operations about systems, and partners (device manufacturers and integrators) are not captured anywhere yet. The repository contains a business capability map from the previous cycle and the operator can use an industry reference model for telecommunications. The sponsor, the director of the B2B division, wants to know within two months which units must be strengthened and which capabilities the company lacks.
question: How should the business architect best proceed in Phase B according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Select the industry reference model and the capability map as inputs, determine the affected and new capabilities, from IoT device management through partner management to B2B billing, and define a value stream for the corporate IoT customer mapped to capabilities. The organization map will show the affected units and partners and the information map the key information; build the baseline, target and gaps on this.

Select the industry reference model and the capability map as inputs, determine the affected and new capabilities (e.g. IoT device management, partner management, B2B billing) and define a value stream for the corporate IoT customer mapped to capabilities. Do not determine the affected units and partners yet, because the organisational arrangement will become clear only during implementation.

Start with detailed modelling of all business and operational processes for the IoT offering in BPMN, so that every unit sees its activities and responsibilities and the disputes over responsibility are settled. Do not use the capability map and the reference model, because they were created for a different purpose and the new offering differs significantly from the operator's existing services.

Adopt as the target Business Architecture the reference solution of the IoT platform supplier, which contains ready-made processes, roles and organisational recommendations for operators. This will significantly shorten Phase B; settle disputes between units according to the supplier's recommendation and give the sponsor its overview of the capabilities needed as the answer to the question of which units to strengthen and which capabilities are missing.
explanation: Phase B begins with selecting reference models, viewpoints and tools and uses Business Architecture techniques: business capabilities show what the enterprise must be able to do, value streams how value for the customer is created, the organization map who (units and partners) takes part in it, and the information map the key information. The best answer combines the existing inputs from the repository with these techniques and aims directly at the dispute about the affected units. The second option uses the techniques, but omits the organization map, so the scenario's main problem remains unresolved. Detailed BPMN without a capability framework is poorly focused; adopting the supplier's architecture is solution selection in Phase B.

scenario: A media group (television channels, a streaming service and news websites) has an approved vision of unified content and rights management: content is processed once and distributed to all channels. Phase C (application architecture) has been running for four months, although it was planned for three. In that time a team of three architects has documented in detail 230 applications of the current state, including all interfaces, but has not yet started work on the target state. Key stakeholders meanwhile agreed on the target concept – a central content hub with a rights management service – at vision level without major disputes. The group wants to succeed with unified rights management in negotiations with licence holders for the next season. The sponsor is dissatisfied and asks when they will see the target architecture.
question: How should the lead architect adjust the approach according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: For this iteration, switch to the target first approach, because the target concept is agreed. Design the target application architecture from the logical components and services of the content hub and rights management, and describe the baseline only to the extent needed for gap analysis and impacts, i.e. only for applications involving content and rights. Use the data already collected and define candidate roadmap components.

Finish documenting the remaining applications of the current state with a reduced level of detail, which will take roughly another two months, and only then design the target application architecture of the content hub and rights management. Then perform gap analysis and define candidate roadmap components; explain to the sponsor that a complete overview of applications will also pay off in later phases and cycles.

Continue the complete documentation of the current state according to plan, because the more detailed the baseline, the more accurate the gap analysis and the smaller the risk of omission. Ask the sponsor to extend Phase C and explain that a quality target architecture requires a complete and detailed description of the starting state, including all interfaces between applications.

Do not produce a target architecture or a gap analysis, and acquire a commercial content hub with rights management, whose implementation team will itself map the existing systems and design the integrations and data flows according to its own methodology. Hand over the documented current state of all 230 applications to the supplier as input, so that the architects' work so far is not wasted and the supplier can start faster.
explanation: TOGAF describes the baseline only to the extent needed for gap analysis and impacts and, for iterations, distinguishes the baseline first and target first approaches; target first suits the situation where the target is agreed at a high level. The best answer therefore switches to target first and limits the baseline to relevant applications. The second option reduces the effort, but still keeps the baseline first approach, which needlessly delays things here. Continuing with the complete baseline is exactly the mistake that caused the situation; skipping the target architecture and gap analysis and leaving the design to the supplier contradicts the ADM.

scenario: An insurance brokerage group has taken over a competitor with 300,000 client contracts and in Phase C is addressing the data architecture for integration into its brokerage platform. The acquired company's master data is in a system whose supplier ends support in six months. The group has 400 employees and mainly serves retail clients. The two companies use different client identifiers, many clients are held in both companies, the acquired company's consents to marketing processing of personal data are in spreadsheets outside the system and the quality of contract data is uncertain. The business wants a single view of the client, and reporting to the regulator must remain correct even during the integration, which is monitored by the board and the group's auditor. The data architect proposes to “map the tables one to one and move everything over a weekend”.
question: What should the data architecture in Phase C focus on according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Describe the baseline and target data architecture at the logical level for client, contract and consent, including their ownership, and address data management including master data, quality and a single view of the client, data migration with cleansing, deduplication, reconciliation and verification, and data governance with data owners, a record of consents and regulatory reporting. Record gaps and requirements in the ARS.

Describe the baseline and target data architecture at the logical level (client, contract, consent) and design the migration including cleansing, deduplication, reconciliation and verification and a single view of the client. Address data ownership, the record of consents and the rules for regulatory reporting only after the migration is completed, when it will be clear what data the group actually has.

Concentrate Phase C on physical mapping (database tables and columns of both systems) and on the design of transfer scripts, because migration is the main risk of the integration and the support end date is approaching. Leave the logical data model and questions of data ownership to the supplier of the brokerage platform, who knows its data model and its limitations in detail.

Accept the data architect's proposal, move the data over a weekend one to one, and resolve duplicates, missing consents and data quality gradually in production (according to client complaints and reporting results). Fast migration will reduce the costs of running both systems in parallel and will safely be completed long before the old system's support ends.
explanation: Phase C (Data) describes the data architecture at the logical level and, according to TOGAF, is explicitly to address data management, data migration and data governance; the results are reflected in the ARS and in candidate roadmap components in line with the application architecture. The best answer covers all three areas including consents and regulatory reporting. The second option addresses management and migration, but postpones data governance, even though consents and reporting are a risk already during integration. Physical table mapping is the wrong level of abstraction; a transfer without analysis and with problems resolved in production contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A regional office is building a shared solution for social work: a client case record shared between the region, municipalities and non-profit organisations. The vision is approved and Phase C (application architecture) begins. The head of the IT department and a supplier representative push for the target application architecture to read straight away “CRM product X plus document management system Y”, because the region already has licences for both products. The solution must communicate with national registries and will be used by social workers of municipalities and non-profit organisations with varying technical equipment. In total there are approximately 1,500 social workers and the ministry is preparing a national standard for data exchange in social services. The data protection officer points to the sensitivity of client data. Among the region's principles is “re-use before buy”.
question: How should the application architecture be created according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Define the target application architecture as logical application components and services for case records, document management, integration with registries and access for municipalities and non-profit organisations, their interactions and links to functions and data, including interoperability with the registries. Record the licences as a constraint or opportunity and assess the products as candidate SBBs only in Phase E.

Define the target application architecture as logical application components and services (case records, document management, access for municipalities and non-profit organisations) and their links to functions and data. Record the licences as a constraint and assess the products in Phase E; leave communication with the national registries to Phase D as a technical integration.

Accept products X and Y as the target application architecture, because the region already has the licences and their use corresponds to the re-use principle, and write the logical components retrospectively according to their functions, so that the documentation is complete. Interoperability with the national registries and access for municipalities and non-profit organisations will then be solved by configuration and extension of both products by their supplier.

Entrust the design of the application architecture to the supplier of products X and Y as part of its implementation offer, because it knows their capabilities, licences and the needs of similar offices in detail. Architects will then merely record the resulting design in the Architecture Definition Document and check its formal completeness, conformance with the approved vision and with the re-use principle.
explanation: Phases B–D define the architecture by means of logical, vendor-independent building blocks (ABBs); specific products (SBBs) are selected only in Phase E, where licensed products can be assessed as candidate solutions. Phase C (Application) also describes how applications share information, so interoperability with registries belongs here. The best answer therefore works with logical components and interoperability and treats the licences as a constraint or opportunity. The second option postpones interoperability to Phase D, where only technical mechanisms are addressed; accepting the products as the target architecture is weak and handing the design to the supplier contradicts TOGAF.
