scenario: A glassworks with three plants wants to reduce furnace energy consumption by 15% using sensors and real-time optimisation. The sponsor is the group's chief technology officer, and the investment is expected to pay back within three years. Phases B and C are complete: target processes and logical application components (data collection, optimisation service, energy reporting). In Phase D, tension emerges between IT and operational technology (OT): the plants' networks are segregated for security reasons, control loops require a response time under 100 ms, group IT has a catalogue of technology standards that prefers the public cloud, and the OT team is wary of the cloud. Nobody has yet decided what will run where. Meanwhile, the OT systems vendor is offering its own "complete IoT platform".
question: How should the technology architect proceed in Phase D according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Select reference models such as the TRM, viewpoints and tools, describe the plants' technology to the necessary extent, and propose a target technology architecture for the logical application and data components, placed at the edge or in the cloud according to latency, security and standards. Together with OT and security, perform a gap analysis, complete the ARS, and assess the vendor's offer only in Phase E.

Select reference models, viewpoints and tools, describe the baseline technology to the necessary extent, and propose a target technology architecture fully in line with the group IT standards catalogue, i.e. with all processing in the public cloud. Perform a gap analysis, define candidate roadmap components and complete the ARS; postpone the OT team's objections until implementation.

Produce detailed physical specifications (plant network diagrams, server sizing, cabling plan), because this is the most labour-intensive part of Phase D and the vendors will need them. The link to the logical application and data components from Phase C and to the vision's objectives does not need to be addressed again in Phase D, because it was confirmed at the formal review of the previous phases.

Let the OT systems vendor design its standard IoT platform, including hardware, edge devices and cloud services, and order it straight away for a pilot plant, because the vendor knows the furnaces and control systems best. Document the technology architecture afterwards, based on the actual platform deployment and pilot results, so that it matches the reality of all three plants exactly.
explanation: Phase D creates a target technology architecture that enables the logical and physical application and data components and the vision; it begins with selecting reference models (e.g. the TRM), viewpoints and tools, considers new technologies, and ends with a gap analysis, candidate roadmap components and requirements in the ARS. The best answer also addresses the scenario's specific constraints (latency, segregated networks) by involving OT. The second option follows the steps but ignores the constraints the scenario explicitly states. Physical detail without a link to the application and data components is misdirected; ordering the vendor's platform and writing the architecture retroactively contradicts the ADM.

scenario: A life insurer is designing, in Phase C, the target architecture of a new client portal that is to go live within twelve months. The target state assumes that the existing CRM will serve as the main source of client data. In parallel, a claims transformation programme with a different sponsor is running; its approved transition architecture assumes the retirement of this CRM within 18 months and its replacement with a new client hub. In addition, the insurer's strategic architecture requires new applications to access data through the integration platform's APIs. The target architectures of all programmes are approved by the insurer's Architecture Board, and the sales director expects the portal to deliver a significant increase in online sales. The portal team did not know about the second programme's plans; it came to light by chance at an informal meeting of architects.
question: What should the lead architect do according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Address the impacts across the Architecture Landscape already in Phase C, because the conflict changes the portal's target state. Analyse the relationship of the target to the second programme's transition architecture and to the strategic architecture, agree with the programme owners on an adjustment of the target with a connection to the new client hub via API, possibly with a temporary solution, bring the disagreements to the Architecture Board, and record the dependencies in the ADD and ARS.

Record the CRM retirement and the API access requirement in the Architecture Requirements Specification and in the candidate roadmap components as a dependency and a risk, and leave their resolution to Phase E, where gaps and dependencies from all domains and programmes are consolidated. Do not change the portal's target state until then, so as not to delay the Phase C schedule or the planned formal review with the portal's stakeholders and its sponsor.

Ask the claims programme to postpone the CRM retirement until the portal is in operation, because the portal has higher priority for the business and brings new revenue. Leave the portal's target architecture unchanged and negotiate the postponement directly with the second programme's architects, so that the Architecture Board does not have to be convened for it.

Do not deal with the second programme (which has a different sponsor), because it is outside the portal's scope, and continue with the target architecture built on the existing CRM. Any problems will be solved when the CRM actually starts being retired, and until then the portal will use a proven and stable source of client data without the risk of depending on another programme.
explanation: The step Resolve Impacts Across the Architecture Landscape in Phases B-D is meant to identify the impacts of the target state on other architectures and projects (including transition and parent architectures) and resolve them before the formal review; conflicts are escalated through governance. The best answer does this in collaboration with the second programme and respects the strategic architecture. The second option records the conflict correctly but postpones its resolution, even though it is already known and changes the target state. A one-sided demand on the other programme negotiated outside governance is weak and ignores the strategic architecture; ignoring the impact contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A construction company with 8,000 employees is completing Phases B-D for a new ERP and construction project management. The ERP is to replace three legacy systems, and site managers will use it daily to enter work performed, materials and changes on construction sites. The implementation partner has been selected and is waiting for inputs. The steering committee, led by the CEO, wants to save three weeks: skip the formal stakeholder review and go straight to Phase E. There are over 300 site managers, but they were involved only at the beginning of Phase B. The new ERP is to go live at the start of the next financial year. The CFO, who is also a member of the steering committee, has meanwhile changed the requirements for job cost reporting because of new group accounting rules, and for several building blocks the rationale for why they were chosen is missing.
question: How should the lead architect proceed according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Conduct a formal stakeholder review against the vision, the SoAW and the current concerns, including the CFO's changed requirements and the site managers' perspective, and save time through targeted views so that the review need not be skipped. Only based on the results, adjust and finalise the architecture, including standards and a complete specification of building blocks with rationale and traceability, and update the ADD and ARS.

Conduct a formal stakeholder review of the target architecture against the vision, the SoAW and the CFO's changed requirements, but only with the steering committee members, to save time and keep the site managers from being pulled away from the sites. Based on the results, adjust and finalise the architecture, including the rationale for building blocks and traceability to requirements, and update the ADD and ARS.

Skip the review now and finalise the architecture in its current form, because the stakeholders, including the site managers, were involved at the beginning of Phase B and the brief has not changed significantly since. Collect the comments of the site managers and the CFO later, together with the review of the roadmap (Phases E and F), when it will be clear how they translate into work packages, and the partner will take them into account in the detailed design.

Skip both the review and the finalisation, hand the ADD over to the ERP implementation partner and let it verify the architecture during implementation, testing and training of the site managers. The partner will fill in the missing rationale for building blocks based on its experience with other construction firms, which is faster and cheaper than another round of architects' work and a review with dozens of stakeholders.
explanation: The steps Conduct Formal Stakeholder Review and Finalize Architecture in Phases B-D verify the architecture against the original motivation and stakeholder concerns and then complete it: standards for building blocks, their complete specification with rationale, and traceability to requirements. The best answer includes the key users and the changed requirements and looks for time savings in a more efficient review. The second option conducts the review, but without the site managers, whose concerns have not been verified since the start of Phase B. Postponing the review until after finalisation is the wrong order; leaving verification and rationale to the implementation partner contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A Czech company operating cloud accounting and payroll software for 40,000 small businesses is preparing a new platform; it will process payroll for roughly 500,000 employees of its clients. The vision with approved security principles and risk appetite is complete and Phase B is starting. Payroll data contains personal data, external accountants need delegated access to the data, and the platform connects to the tax authority and banks. Payment of salaries in thousands of companies will depend on the platform, so an outage or data leak would have a major impact. After last year's incident at a competitor, customers demand evidence of security. The platform is to be launched in fourteen months. The CISO proposes to "insert a list of ISO 27001 controls into the ARS in Phase D", and the developers want to select a specific identity management product already now.
question: How should security be addressed in Phases B-D according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: In Phase B, perform a risk assessment and create a security domain model, a trust framework for the trust relationships between clients, accountants, the tax authority and banks, and a register of relevant laws and regulations. In Phase C, define data classification and security services as ABBs, including identity management with delegated access. In Phase D, verify the effectiveness of the controls, and select products only in Phase E.

In Phase C, define security services as ABBs (e.g. identity management with delegated access, audit logs) and data classification; in Phase D, ensure the presence and effectiveness of controls and record the requirements in the ARS; select products only in Phase E. Do not create business security artefacts in Phase B, because the principles and risk appetite have already been approved in the vision.

Accept the CISO's proposal and in Phase D insert the complete list of ISO 27001 controls into the ARS as security requirements for the platform. Do not deal with security separately in Phases B and C, because the controls from the standard cover all areas and their fulfilment can easily be demonstrated later by a certification audit, including to customers who demand it after the competitor's incident.

Comply with the developers: select the identity management product immediately; derive the security architecture, roles, permissions and the accountants' delegated access from its default configuration and the vendor's recommendations. Time is saved, security rests on a proven and certified solution, and the developers can start implementing login right away.
explanation: According to G152, each of Phases B-D has its own security work: in Phase B, among other things, a risk assessment, a security domain model, a trust framework and a register of laws and regulations; in Phase C, security services as ABBs and data classification; in Phase D, verification of the presence and effectiveness of controls; products (SBBs) come into play only in Phase E. The best answer covers all three phases and specifically addresses delegated access. The second option omits business security in Phase B, so the trust relationships between participants remain undefined. A list of controls from a standard instead of a risk-based design is weak; deriving the security architecture from a product contradicts TOGAF.

scenario: A national motorway and road authority is completing Phases B-D for intelligent traffic management: sensors, a traffic control centre and data sharing with navigation services. The centre is to be operational within three years and the project is funded from European funds. The traffic police, regional road administrators and navigation service providers are involved in the project. The team has created dozens of diagrams in a modelling tool. The project office wants to start Phase E next week and prepare the tender documentation, and therefore asks "what exactly must the suppliers meet". A check showed that the results of the gap analysis are not captured anywhere in summary form, requirements exist only in meeting minutes in the form "the system must be fast and reliable", requirements for data exchange with the navigation services and for national standards are not documented, and the candidate roadmap components are missing.
question: What should the lead architect ensure before moving to Phase E according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Update the Architecture Definition Document (baseline and target, views, rationale, gap analysis and impacts) and compile the Architecture Requirements Specification with measurable and testable requirements, interoperability and standards, constraints and assumptions. Define candidate roadmap components from the gaps and formally review everything so that Phase E has complete inputs.

Update the Architecture Definition Document (baseline, target, views, rationale, gap analysis results) and compile the Architecture Requirements Specification with measurable requirements, interoperability requirements, constraints and assumptions. Do not define candidate roadmap components, because Phase E will derive work packages from the gaps anyway.

Insert all diagrams from the tool into the Architecture Definition Document and attach the meeting minutes as a list of requirements. The project office thus receives complete documentation without further delay, and the suppliers will refine the requirements in their bids, which is common practice in public procurement and saves the architects' time.

Start Phase E with a request for information (RFI) to suppliers, in which they themselves propose the requirements and the solution for the sensors, the traffic control centre and data sharing with the navigation services, and complete the architecture based on their responses. Suppliers know what is technically achievable, and the tender documentation will therefore match what the market actually offers and the requirements of the European funds.
explanation: The outputs of Phases B-D needed to proceed are an updated ADD (a qualitative description of the architecture including gap analysis and impacts), a draft ARS (quantitative, testable requirements including interoperability, constraints and assumptions) and candidate roadmap components for each domain. It is the ARS that answers the question of what the implementation must meet. The second option omits the candidate roadmap components, which are an input to the consolidation in Phase E. Diagrams and minutes without testable requirements are a weak substitute; letting suppliers define the requirements contradicts TOGAF.

scenario:
A mid-sized Czech bank is modernising its consumer lending process. The architecture team has completed Phases B, C and D: the business architecture assumes digital approval and new roles for credit analysts, the data architecture assumes unifying client data from three systems, and the application and technology architecture assumes replacing the obsolete lending system, a new scoring module and an API layer.

Each domain architect has submitted their own list of gaps. Many gaps overlap (the same client data problem appears in both the data and the application list) and some solutions depend on each other - for example, the new scoring cannot work without unified client data. The CIO must present a roadmap to the steering committee in six weeks. The PMO lead proposes setting up a project for every item from all three lists and immediately issuing a tender for the new lending system so that no time is lost. The chief architect is just starting Phase E (Opportunities and Solutions).
question: How should the chief architect proceed next according to the TOGAF Standard?
options: Consolidate the gaps from Phases B-D into the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions, and Dependencies Matrix: merge overlaps, add possible solutions and validate dependencies, because scoring needs unified data. Record constraints in the Implementation Factor Catalog and only then group work packages, identify Transition Architectures and compile the first complete Architecture Roadmap.

Merge the three gap lists into the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions, and Dependencies Matrix and, by domain, group work packages straight from it into the first version of the Architecture Roadmap, so that the CIO can present it to the steering committee in time. Work out the dependencies between solutions and the constraints in detail only in Phase F, when project resources and schedules are estimated.

Keep the three domain gap lists separate and compile a separate partial roadmap for each domain with its own work packages, which can then simply be shown in the Architecture Roadmap alongside the others. The overlaps and dependencies between domains will be resolved by the project managers during delivery within Phase G (Implementation Governance).

Accept the PMO's proposal: set up a project for every gap from all three lists and immediately issue tenders for the new lending system, the scoring module and the API layer, which gives the bank time. The outputs of Phases B-D will serve the suppliers as the brief, the Architecture Roadmap will be compiled afterwards based on the schedules in their bids, and the architects will get involved only at acceptance.
explanation: Phase E begins with consolidating the gap analysis results from Phases B-D and validating dependencies (the steps Review and Consolidate Gap Analysis Results from Phases B to D and Refine and Validate Dependencies); the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions, and Dependencies Matrix and the Implementation Factor Catalog serve this purpose. Only then are work packages grouped and Transition Architectures identified. The 3-point option uses the matrix but postpones dependencies to Phase F, even though they determine the order of work packages. Separate domain roadmaps (1 point) resolve neither overlaps nor dependencies and push them onto the projects; adopting the PMO's proposal (0 points) skips planning in Phase E and lets suppliers determine the roadmap.

scenario:
A network of four regional hospitals is unifying its hospital information systems: four different systems are to be replaced by one shared system, connected to a new laboratory application and to national e-health services. Phases B-D are approved and the chief architect is working in Phase E.

The Business Transformation Readiness Assessment from Phase A showed low readiness: the IT department has only a few people, nurses are overloaded, and the previous introduction of electronic documentation three years ago ended in a return to paper. Since then, the management of two hospitals has also changed. The hospitals run around the clock and downtime of key systems is possible only for a matter of hours; the region as founder requires that patient care not be put at risk during the change. The CEO wants to switch all four hospitals at once on 1 January to save the licences of the old systems. The vendor of the new system supports both hospital-by-hospital deployment and a one-time cutover.
question: How should the chief architect approach formulating the Implementation and Migration Strategy?
options: Build on the readiness assessment from Phase A, confirm the readiness and risks of the transformation in the current situation and propose mitigations. Recommend an evolutionary approach (Evolutionary) with deployment hospital by hospital so that care is not put at risk, define Transition Architectures with measurable value, and discuss the strategy with management and the heads of departments.

Recommend an evolutionary approach (Evolutionary) with gradual deployment hospital by hospital, define Transition Architectures with measurable business value, and discuss the strategy with management and the heads of departments. Do not reassess readiness and transformation risks again, because the Capability Assessment from Phase A is approved and its conclusions apply unchanged.

Comply with the CEO: choose a revolutionary approach (Revolutionary) with a one-time cutover of all four hospitals on 1 January, which will bring the fastest licence savings. Reduce the risks through intensive staff training and enhanced vendor support in the first weeks; Transition Architectures are not needed for a one-time cutover.

Shorten Phase E and leave the method of deployment, the order of the hospitals and the dates of downtime to the vendor of the new system, which has the most experience with hospitals and follows its own proven methodology. The architecture team will get involved only in the compliance reviews in Phase G (Implementation Governance), when it is already clear how the vendor has planned the deployment and what risks it anticipates.
explanation: Phase E contains the step Confirm Readiness and Risk for Business Transformation, which follows up on the readiness assessment from Phase A; the choice of the Implementation and Migration Strategy rests on its result. With low readiness and continuous operation, an evolutionary approach with Transition Architectures is appropriate, each delivering measurable value, and the strategy needs to be discussed with stakeholders. The 3-point option chooses the right approach but omits confirming readiness and risks, even though the situation has changed since Phase A. A revolutionary cutover (1 point) ignores the identified low readiness, and handing the strategy to the vendor (0 points) gives up architectural planning.

scenario:
A logistics company operating twelve warehouses in the Czech Republic and Slovakia is modernising warehouse management. The target architecture includes a new WMS, shipment tracking using IoT sensors, a customer portal and a data platform for capacity planning. The change is too extensive for a single step, and the team is therefore preparing Transition Architectures in Phase E.

The domain architects proposed transition states at six-month intervals according to the IT release calendar; each state is described by a list of technical deliverables, for example "database migration" or "integration platform deployment". The chief operating officer, who is the programme sponsor and must demonstrate benefits to the board every quarter, and the sales director complain that they cannot see from the plan when the company will gain which capabilities - for example, when key customers will be able to track shipments online. Several projects (WMS, portal, data platform) are working on the same capabilities, and their deliverables must follow on from one another.
question: How should the chief architect adjust the approach to Transition Architectures?
options: Define Transition Architectures as architecturally significant states, each delivering measurable business value (e.g. online shipment tracking), and keep the IT release calendar only as a constraint; discuss the transitions with the sponsors. Assign projects to increments in the Architecture Definition Increments Table and show the state of building blocks in the Transition Architecture State Evolution Table.

Keep the six-month transition states according to the IT release calendar, but add to each a description of the expected business benefit for the chief operating officer and the sales director. Capture the sequencing of projects in the Architecture Definition Increments Table, the state of building blocks in the Transition Architecture State Evolution Table, and reflect both in the Architecture Roadmap.

Keep the technically defined transition states, because they match the IT release plan and the capacity of the development teams well, and explain to the sponsors that business value will fully materialise only once the target architecture is reached. Ensure project coordination through a joint schedule in the Implementation and Migration Plan prepared by the PMO. A separate benefits overview for the whole programme can be prepared for the sponsors.

Let each project (WMS, portal, data platform) define its own transition states according to its release plans and compile the Architecture Roadmap as a summary of these plans. The architecture team thus eliminates unnecessary coordination, projects gain freedom in the order of deliveries, and sponsors see dates directly from the projects. Each project will thus have clear responsibility for its deliverables.
explanation: Transition Architectures describe architecturally significant states between the baseline and the target, and each is meant to deliver measurable business value; the intervals between them need not be equal. The link of projects to increments and the evolution of building blocks across transitions are supported by the Architecture Definition Increments Table and the Transition Architecture State Evolution Table. The 3-point option uses these tools, but transitions are still determined by the release calendar and value is merely written onto them. Technical transitions without value (1 point) contradict the purpose of Transition Architectures, and splitting the roadmap into independent project plans (0 points) removes the coordination the scenario requires.

scenario:
After Phase E, an insurer has an Architecture Roadmap with nine work packages, including digital claims reporting, a new contract administration system, CRM, a data warehouse and a migration to the cloud. Next year's budget will cover roughly half of them. The directors of the non-life and life insurance divisions claim that their own packages are the most important, and the CIO pushes for priority migration to the cloud because of technical debt.

In the past, the order of projects was decided by who was loudest on the steering committee, and several projects then delivered little benefit. The Architecture Board therefore asked the chief architect to prepare a defensible order of migration projects for the investment committee, which meets in a month. The chief architect is working in Phase F (Migration Planning) and has at their disposal the approved Architecture Vision with objectives and KPIs and the cost estimates from Phase E.
question: What approach should the chief architect choose?
options: Assign business value to each work package according to agreed criteria (return on investment, critical success factors, strategic alignment) and assess its risks in the Business Value and Risk Matrix. Prioritise the migration projects according to cost/benefit and risk assessment, taking resources and dependencies into account, and discuss the order with stakeholders and the Architecture Board so that it is defensible.

Assign business value to each work package according to return on investment and strategic alignment and rank the projects from the highest value, so that the order is easy to understand. Leave risks, resource availability and mutual dependencies to the individual projects, which will assess them in their own planning, and discuss the resulting order with the Architecture Board.

Rank the projects solely by technical dependencies in the Architecture Roadmap (first the migration to the cloud and the data warehouse as a common foundation, then the other packages by completion date). There is no need to quantify the business value of individual work packages, because they all derive from the approved Architecture Vision.

Decide the order alone, according to which work package brings the architecturally clean target state closest, and present it to the investment committee as a finished recommendation without alternatives and without discussion. The division directors will adjust their expectations, because architecture must take precedence over the partial interests of individual divisions. The investment committee thus receives a clear recommendation without unnecessary compromises.
explanation: Phase F requires assigning business value to each work package (Assign a Business Value to Each Work Package) and prioritising migration projects using cost/benefit and risk assessment; a helpful tool is the Business Value and Risk Matrix (in the 2022 version, the Business Value Assessment Technique), which sets value against risk. The best answer also takes resources and dependencies into account and validates the order with stakeholders. The 3-point option assigns value but omits risks and dependencies, so the order may be unfeasible. Ranking solely by technical dependencies (1 point) ignores business value, and the architect's unilateral decision (0 points) contradicts the principle that the architect provides the inputs and that authorised stakeholders decide on priorities.

scenario:
An automotive components manufacturer with three plants has completed Phase E of a manufacturing digitalisation programme (a new MES, predictive maintenance, integration with customers' systems). The company has an established PMO that plans projects according to an annual budget cycle (the budget is approved in October), group-level portfolio management, and operational IT managed according to ITIL. The production director plans line shutdowns two years ahead.

The company did not use the previous architecture plan: the schedule did not match the budget cycle, the PMO planned the projects its own way, and operations were not ready to take over the new systems, so two of them ran for months without support. The chief architect is now starting Phase F and has at their disposal the Architecture Roadmap with work packages and Transition Architectures and the high-level Implementation and Migration Plan from Phase E. The CEO requires that this time the plan pass the budget round without additional changes.
question: What should the chief architect start Phase F with so that the mistake from last time is not repeated?
options: Confirm the interactions of the Implementation and Migration Plan with the other management frameworks so that the plan passes the budget round. Align the work packages with the budget cycle together with the PMO and portfolio management, agree on the takeover of systems with operations managed according to ITIL, and agree shutdown dates with production. Only then assign business value, estimate resources and complete the plan.

First complete a detailed Implementation and Migration Plan with a project schedule and resource estimates, and only then present the finished plan to the PMO, portfolio management and operations so that they can incorporate it into their processes. Resolve any mismatches with the budget cycle and shutdown dates through change control of the plan.

Hand the Architecture Roadmap directly to the PMO, which will derive the project schedule from it itself according to its own rules and the budget cycle, because project planning is its exclusive responsibility. The architect will return to the plan only at the compliance reviews in Phase G, when it will be clear which projects received budget.

Declare the Implementation and Migration Plan the binding project plan that takes precedence over the processes of the PMO, portfolio management and the budget cycle, because it is derived from the approved architecture. Operations will adapt to the deadlines, the production director will adjust the shutdown plan, and the PMO will merely administer the plan.
explanation: The first step of Phase F is Confirm Management Framework Interactions for the Implementation and Migration Plan: the plan must be aligned with portfolio and project management, the budget cycle, operations and the enterprise's other management frameworks, otherwise it will remain unused. Only then follow the assignment of business value, resource estimation, prioritisation and completion of the plan. The 3-point option produces the right output but performs the coordination only afterwards, which is exactly the mistake of the past. Handing the roadmap to the PMO without completing the plan (1 point) abandons the responsibility of Phase F, and placing the architecture plan above the other frameworks (0 points) contradicts the principle that TOGAF integrates with other management frameworks and does not replace them.

scenario:
An electricity distributor is completing Phase F of a smart metering programme that includes replacing hundreds of thousands of electricity meters, a new data collection platform and connection to the systems of electricity traders. Implementation will be delivered by three external suppliers (a system integrator, a meter manufacturer and a cloud platform provider) and an internal agile team.

In the previous programme, the architects lost oversight once delivery began: suppliers made design decisions that undermined the target architecture, and nobody knew who was allowed to approve deviations. The programme director asks what must be ready before the projects are launched. The Architecture Roadmap and the Implementation and Migration Plan are almost complete, and the procurement department is already concluding commercial contracts with the suppliers with prices, deadlines and penalties. The internal team works in two-week sprints and wants to know how it will be involved in architectural oversight. The Architecture Board meets once a month, and its chair wants to have an overview of deviations before they show up in costs.
question: What should the chief architect prepare at the end of Phase F so that the transition to implementation is controlled?
options: Complete the Implementation and Migration Plan and create an Implementation Governance Model with processes, roles and decision rights, including approval of deviations by the Board and checkpoints for compliance reviews. Also prepare draft Architecture Contracts for the suppliers and the internal team, because commercial contracts do not address the architecture. Sign them only in Phase G.

Complete the Implementation and Migration Plan and create an Implementation Governance Model with roles, decision rights and checkpoints for compliance reviews. Do not prepare Architecture Contracts, because the commercial contracts concluded by the procurement department already contain deadlines, prices and penalties, and architectural requirements can be added to them later if need be.

Sign Architecture Contracts with the suppliers already in Phase F so that they are binding before work begins, and entrust ongoing oversight of the architecture to the project managers of the individual suppliers, who know their deliverables best. The architects will be available to the projects for consultation on request. The architects will thus not delay deliveries.

Hand the Architecture Definition Document and the Architecture Requirements Specification to the suppliers and leave further steps to them; the ADM cycle for Phase F ends and the architects move on to the next programme. Any deviations from the target architecture will be dealt with only in Phase H, if they show up in operation. Responsibility for compliance will thereby pass to the suppliers.
explanation: The output of Phase F is, besides the final Implementation and Migration Plan, also the Implementation Governance Model, which ensures that the transition to implementation is at the same time a transition under proper governance, with processes, roles, checkpoints and success criteria. The draft Architecture Contract is an input to Phase G, where it is signed and used to communicate gaps, specifications and oversight to implementers. The 3-point option has the governance model but omits Architecture Contracts, even though uncontrolled supplier decisions were exactly the problem; a commercial contract does not replace architectural requirements. Entrusting oversight to the suppliers (1 point) and omitting governance entirely (0 points) repeat the failure of the previous programme.

scenario:
A regional authority is digitalising services for citizens and municipalities: a new portal for submitting applications, an electronic records management service for all departments, a connection to the national identity service, and the replacement of several line-of-business systems. In Phase E, the team has consolidated gaps from Phases B-D.

The existing records management service is used by two departments, and the vendor offers to extend it to the entire authority; two line-of-business systems are stable and supported, three are at the end of their life. Every purchase is subject to the public procurement act and a tender takes nine to twelve months. Part of the funding comes from a European grant that must be spent by the end of 2028. Department heads push for each department to have everything custom-developed by the internal development team, which, however, has only eight developers. In addition, the regional governor has publicly promised that the first portal services will be available to citizens within one year.
question: How should the chief architect identify and group the major work packages?
options: For each gap, determine whether it will be new development, reuse of an existing solution (records management service, national identity service) or a purchase, and classify the existing systems as Mainstream, Contain or Replace. Record the procurement deadlines and the grant deadline in the Implementation Factor Catalog, because they determine feasibility, and group the work packages according to them and according to dependencies.

For each gap, determine whether the solution will be new development, reuse of an existing product or a purchase, classify the existing systems as Mainstream, Contain or Replace, and group the work packages by the functional proximity of the solutions. Deal with the public procurement deadlines and the grant spending deadline only when the individual projects are delivered.

Group the work packages by the authority's departments so that each department has its own package and clear responsibility for the result, and let the project managers decide on the method of delivery (development, purchase or reuse of an existing solution). Leave the existing line-of-business systems unchanged until the new portal is complete and verified. The departments will thus have full control over their packages.

Comply with the department heads: have all solutions custom-developed by the internal team, because in-house development guarantees the best fit with requirements and avoids lengthy tenders. Do not use existing products or shared national services, so that the authority is not dependent on suppliers and on state systems. The internal team also knows the departments' needs well.
explanation: In the step Identify and Group Major Work Packages, the method of solution is determined for each gap (new development, reuse of an existing solution, purchase) and existing systems are classified as Mainstream, Contain or Replace; constraints such as procurement deadlines or the grant spending deadline belong in the Implementation Factor Catalog and influence both the grouping and the order of the packages. The 3-point option proceeds correctly but disregards the constraints that fundamentally determine feasibility in the scenario. Grouping by departments with the solution decision postponed (1 point) follows neither the logic of the solutions nor dependencies. Custom development of everything without using existing and shared solutions (0 points) goes against reuse and ignores the capacity and constraints from the scenario.

scenario:
A health insurer is replacing the system for processing healthcare claims. The target architecture assumes online exchange of structured data with hospitals and with the national e-health system, and this requirement is recorded in the Architecture Requirements Specification.

In Phase E, it turned out that the packaged solution preferred by the business for its functionality can exchange data only in batches via files once a day. The vendor offers extensive customisation, IT proposes an integration layer that would convert the batches into an online interface, and hospital representatives ask whether they will have to change their interfaces. The security manager points out that temporary solutions for exchanging sensitive health data tend to be a weak spot and must meet personal data protection requirements. The chief architect is just preparing the Architecture Roadmap and the Implementation and Migration Plan. The hospitals have their own information system vendors, and any interface change takes them several months.
question: How should the chief architect deal with the identified conflict?
options: In the step Consolidate and Reconcile Interoperability Requirements, compare the required interoperability with the package's capabilities and evaluate the alternatives (customisation, integration layer, another product) in terms of cost, risk and security. Leave the decision to the affected stakeholders, including the hospitals, because their interfaces are also at stake, and reflect it in the ARS, ADD and roadmap.

Compare the required level of interoperability with the package's capabilities and evaluate the alternatives (customisation, integration layer, another product) in terms of cost, risk and security. Make the decision only with the insurer's internal business and IT; inform the hospitals and the national system operator of the interface change only before deployment.

Record the conflict as a risk in the Implementation Factor Catalog and continue with the preferred package in the Architecture Roadmap. Leave the specific way of achieving online exchange to the vendor, who will describe it in the Architecture Contract, and then verify its fulfilment through a compliance review in Phase G.

Without further assessment, lower the requirement in the Architecture Requirements Specification to a once-daily batch exchange so that it matches the preferred package, and continue with the roadmap according to the original plan. Announce the change to the hospitals and the national system operator at deployment, because the business has already chosen the package. This also avoids both costly customisation of the package and the integration layer.
explanation: Phase E contains the step Consolidate and Reconcile Interoperability Requirements, in which interoperability requirements are compared with the constraints of potential solutions, typically COTS packages. The conflict is resolved by evaluating alternatives, including cost, risk and security, and by a decision of the stakeholders affected by the data exchange; the result is reflected in the ARS, ADD and roadmap. The 3-point option leaves out the external stakeholders, even though their interfaces are at stake. Deferring the conflict to the vendor and Phase G (1 point) shifts an architectural decision to the implementer, and silently lowering the requirement (0 points) bypasses governance and the affected stakeholders.

scenario:
A retail chain with 300 stores and an e-shop is preparing next year's budget. The Architecture to Support Portfolio identified several high-value work packages in the Architecture Roadmap: personalised offers, an online overview of in-store stock for omnichannel sales, and a new loyalty programme.

However, the same IT team must carry out an ERP upgrade next year, the stores cannot accept changes to checkout processes before Christmas, and omnichannel sales depend on cleansing the master product data, which has not yet started. The CEO wants to deliver all the high-value packages next year, the CFO needs a realistic budget proposal within six weeks, and store managers point to change fatigue after last year's introduction of new tills. The chief architect is to prepare a recommendation for the budget discussion. The CFO also points out that the change budget will be one tenth lower than this year's.
question: What recommendation should the chief architect prepare?
options: Group the work packages into themes and balance opportunity, i.e. business value, against feasibility: the IT team's capacity alongside the ERP upgrade, store readiness, risks and dependencies (master data first). Estimate resources and timing, including the pre-Christmas change freeze, and present options with value, cost and risk to management for a decision.

Rank the work packages by business value and dependencies, so that master data cleansing goes first, and estimate resources taking into account the IT team's capacity alongside the ERP upgrade. Present options with value, cost and risk to management; leave store readiness and the pre-Christmas period to the planning of the individual projects.

Recommend delivering all high-value packages (from personalisation through omnichannel to the loyalty programme) next year, as the CEO wants, and solve the shortage of IT team capacity by hiring external suppliers. Risks and store readiness will be managed by the individual projects within their own risk management, and the Architecture Roadmap will be updated accordingly.

Postpone the budget recommendation until a detailed target architecture, down to the level of specific solutions, has been produced for all work packages, i.e. personalisation, omnichannel, the loyalty programme and the ERP upgrade, so that the estimates are accurate. The budget discussion will do without architectural input until then, and the projects will wait for the finished documentation.
explanation: At the portfolio level, according to G186, work packages are grouped into themes and opportunity (business value) is balanced against feasibility - capacity, readiness, risks and dependencies - and the result is prepared for the budget decision; Phase F adds resource and timing estimation and prioritisation by cost, benefit and risk. The 3-point option works with value, dependencies and capacity, but omits store readiness and the pre-Christmas restriction, which the scenario explicitly mentions. Recommending everything at once (1 point) ignores feasibility and shifts the risks onto the projects. Postponing until a detailed architecture is produced (0 points) misses the budget cycle - architecture delivered after the decision will no longer influence anything.

scenario:
A chemical plant is modernising production control: the existing MES and the line control systems (OT) are to be connected to a new cloud platform for data analysis and predictive maintenance. Phases B-D are approved and the chief architect is preparing the migration approach in Phases E and F.

During the transition, which will last about a year, the old and the new MES will run in parallel and temporary interfaces will arise between the OT network and the cloud. The security manager (CISO) points out that the transition period itself opens new attack paths, and reminds everyone that the plant is subject to cybersecurity regulation. Production may be stopped for at most eight hours per quarter, and the owners of operational risks are the heads of the individual operations. The platform vendor offers to take over the security of the transition as part of its solution, and management is considering this offer because it would shorten planning. Plant management wants the migration plan approved by the end of the quarter.
question: How should the chief architect handle the security of the migration in Phases E and F?
options: Treat migration as a process that needs to be secured, because transitional states open new attack paths. Assess the risks of each Transition Architecture, including the temporary interfaces and parallel running, consult them with the risk owners and the CISO, and prepare a Risk Mitigation Plan for the transition with back-out plans. Reflect the results in the roadmap and the I&M Plan.

Assess the risks of the target architecture with the CISO and the risk owners, prepare a Risk Mitigation Plan and reflect it in the Architecture Roadmap and the Implementation and Migration Plan, including downtime windows. Do not assess the temporary interfaces and parallel running during the transition in detail or separately, because it is a short-term state that will disappear once the migration is complete.

Address security only in Phase G: before each deployment step, carry out a security audit and penetration tests, and leave a time reserve in the Implementation and Migration Plan for remediating findings. In Phases E and F, concentrate on the migration schedule and on limiting production downtime to eight hours per quarter. The tests will show the actual security state of the systems.

Accept the vendor's offer and contractually transfer responsibility for the security of the transition to it, because it knows the platform best. Architecture does not deal with the security of operations, and the heads of operations can accept any risks informally so that the migration is not needlessly delayed by approvals. The plant will thus have a single responsible partner for security.
explanation: According to G152, migration is itself a process that needs to be secured: in Phases E and F, the risks of the transition are assessed, a Risk Mitigation Plan limited to the transition period is created, a return (back-out) is planned together with a security impact analysis, and risk owners are consulted. The 3-point option correctly works with the risks of the target but overlooks precisely the transitional states the CISO points out. Moving security to testing in Phase G (1 point) turns it into an afterthought check instead of part of the design. Transferring responsibility to the vendor and informal risk acceptance (0 points) bypass governance and the risk owners.

scenario:
An online seller of sporting goods has completed Phase F: the Implementation and Migration Plan, the Implementation Governance Model and the draft Architecture Contracts are approved. The programme comprises four projects - a new checkout, a connection to the payment gateway, integration with an external warehouse and a new CRM - delivered by two external suppliers and internal development teams.

Because of the approaching Black Friday, the head of development has meanwhile changed priorities: he wants to deliver only the new checkout first and postpone the other projects. One of the suppliers has also announced that the key specialist for payment integrations will be available only in three months. The suppliers are waiting for the instruction to start work, and management is asking when implementation will begin. The chief architect is responsible for Phase G (Implementation Governance) and knows that the checkout cannot go live without payment integration. Nobody has signed the Architecture Contracts yet.
question: What should the chief architect do at the start of Phase G?
options: Confirm the scope and deployment priorities with the head of development - the shift due to Black Friday and the fact that the checkout cannot go live without payments - and reflect the change in the plan through governance. Identify resources and skills (the missing payments specialist) and only on the basis of the updated plan complete and sign the Architecture Contracts and plan the compliance reviews.

Together with the suppliers and internal teams, complete and sign the Architecture Contracts according to the original Implementation and Migration Plan and plan the compliance reviews according to the Implementation Governance Model. Deal with the change of priorities due to Black Friday and the specialist's unavailability only during delivery as a change request, once their impacts show up.

Immediately start compliance reviews of the suppliers' existing designs in order to catch deviations as early as possible, and sign the Architecture Contracts later (they are more of a formality). Accept the head of development's change of priorities without further discussion, because he is responsible for delivery. It can formally be incorporated into the plan afterwards within governance, if necessary.

Take over technical leadership of the new checkout project and design the solution directly in the architecture team, so that conformance with the target architecture is guaranteed. Architecture Contracts and compliance reviews are then unnecessary, because the architects themselves create the solution and the suppliers merely provide capacity. The architects also know the target architecture in detail.
explanation: Phase G begins with the steps Confirm Scope and Priorities for Deployment with Development Management and Identify Deployment Resources and Skills; only then does the architect guide the development of the solution, sign Architecture Contracts and conduct compliance reviews according to the Implementation Governance Model. The 3-point option takes the right steps but ignores the change of priorities and the missing resources, so the contracts are created on top of an invalid plan. Reviews without signed contracts and without agreed priorities (1 point) lack the agreed framework against which conformance is assessed. The architects taking over development (0 points) contradicts the principle that in Phase G architects oversee and govern conformance but do not build the solution.

scenario:
A bank is implementing a new mobile banking backend which, because of a regulatory deadline, must be in operation within three months. During development, the supplier used a message broker that is not in the Standards Library - the bank's standard is a different integration platform. The compliance review revealed the deviation.

The project manager claims it is a temporary solution: the team knows the platform, switching to the standard would jeopardise the deadline, and after launch the application would be migrated to the standard platform. The head of IT operations points out that his team has no experience with the broker and that parallel support of two platforms means costs and operational risk. The security department has not yet assessed the broker. The Architecture Contract with the supplier refers to the Standards Library. The chief architect is preparing materials for the next Architecture Board meeting, which takes place in a week. The Board rejected a similar deviation on another project last year because a migration plan was missing.
question: How should the chief architect handle the deviation?
options: Record the deviation in the Compliance Assessment, assess with operations and security the impacts on support, the risks and the cost of migration, and leave the decision to the Architecture Board, because exceptions to standards are granted only by the Board - e.g. a time-limited dispensation with conditions (migration deadline, operational support, monitoring) reflected in the Architecture Contract.

Record the deviation in the Compliance Assessment and present it to the Architecture Board with a proposal for a time-limited dispensation with a fixed deadline for migration to the standard platform, reflected in the Architecture Contract. Deal with the impacts on IT operations and the security of the broker only after launch, because the temporary solution will run for only a short time.

Declare the solution Non-conformant and, citing the Architecture Contract, insist on an immediate switch to the standard platform, because standards must be followed. The risk of missing the regulatory deadline is the project's responsibility, and there is no need to involve the Architecture Board, because the standard is unambiguous.

Given the regulatory deadline, silently accept the deviation and record it nowhere (the project did promise a migration after launch). There is no need to burden the Architecture Board or operations, temporary solutions are common, and a Compliance Assessment would needlessly delay approval of deployment. The bank would also show the regulator that it takes regulatory deadlines truly seriously.
explanation: A deviation identified in a compliance review must be recorded in the Compliance Assessment and presented to the Architecture Board; the Board may grant a dispensation, i.e. a formal, time-limited exception with conditions, which it then monitors. The best answer prepares the decision including the impacts on operations and security, which the scenario explicitly mentions. The 3-point option chooses the right mechanism but postpones these impacts, so the Board decides without key information. Unilaterally enforcing the standard without the Board (1 point) ignores the business deadline and the dispensation mechanism, and silently accepting the deviation (0 points) bypasses governance entirely.

scenario:
A group of three hospitals is building a new patient portal with appointment booking, access to medical records and a connection to the national e-health services. The portal is delivered by an external supplier at a fixed price; the Implementation Governance Model from Phase F provides for compliance reviews but does not specify their timing.

The project manager proposes carrying out a single review just before launch, so as not to hold up the supplier. In the previous project, it was precisely at the final review that it was discovered that the supplier had built its own identity management instead of the enterprise solution, and remediation took four months. The Architecture Board wants a continuous overview of the state of conformance, and the data protection officer points to the sensitivity of health data. The supplier delivers in four stages and will submit the first solution design in six weeks. The chief architect is to propose how the compliance reviews will run. The supplier agrees with the project manager's proposal, because every review costs it time.
question: How should the chief architect set up compliance reviews for this project?
options: Schedule compliance reviews at key milestones - after the initial design, upon a significant design change and before launch - so that deviations are caught in time, and adapt their scope to the project's risks (identity, integration, health data). Process the results into a Compliance Assessment for the Architecture Board and address findings through remediation, dispensation or a change request.

Schedule compliance reviews at key milestones - after the initial design, upon a significant change and before launch - with a scope adapted to the risks (identity, integration, health data). Share the results of the interim reviews only within the project and present to the Architecture Board only the summary Compliance Assessment from the pre-launch review.

Comply with the project manager: carry out a single compliance review before launch, but a very thorough one, with all checklists and with the participation of the security team and the data protection officer. Present the resulting Compliance Assessment to the Architecture Board, which will decide on any remediation or dispensation.

Omit formal compliance reviews and rely on the supplier's declaration of conformance with the architecture, which is part of the commercial contract, on acceptance tests and on the project manager's check of the delivered functionality. The architects need not interfere in the work of the supplier, which is responsible for the result, including identity management and data protection, within the fixed price.
explanation: Compliance reviews should take place at project milestones (e.g. after the initial design, upon a major design change, before launch), because errors caught earlier are cheaper and less risky; the scope of the review is adapted to the project and the output is a Compliance Assessment for governance. The 3-point option has the right timing but deprives the Architecture Board of the continuous overview it explicitly requests. A single thorough review at the end (1 point) repeats the mistake of the previous project, when a fundamental deviation was discovered late. Relying on the supplier's declaration (0 points) removes the independent conformance check and thereby the point of Implementation Governance.

scenario:
A water utility has commissioned an external integrator to develop a new asset management system (water networks, pumping stations) and connect it to GIS, billing and the customer portal. The procurement department has concluded a commercial contract with price, deadlines and penalties. The integrator asks what exactly the requirement for "conformance with the enterprise architecture", which the contract mentions in only one sentence, means.

The previous supplier of a different system passed all functional acceptance tests but built its own customer database, thereby violating the principle of a single source of customer data, and the fix cost hundreds of thousands. A draft Architecture Contract from Phase F exists, but it contains only general references to documents. The chief architect is starting Phase G, and the programme sponsor, the chief technology officer, wants to be sure the situation will not be repeated. The integrator is to start development in three weeks and has so far received only the Architecture Definition Document, without an explanation of which of its parts are binding for it.
question: How should the chief architect use the Architecture Contract?
options: Elaborate the draft Architecture Contract and agree it with the integrator and the sponsor so that it is clear what is binding. Include in the contract the scope, the principles including a single source of customer data, the requirements and conformance requirements from the ARS, the stage deliverables and target metrics, the way compliance reviews are conducted and how changes are handled. Sign the contract only in Phase G and link it with the commercial contract.

Attach the Architecture Definition Document and the Architecture Requirements Specification to the commercial contract as annexes and require the integrator in writing to deliver a solution conforming to them, without further jointly clarifying the content. Verify conformance through compliance reviews at project milestones and present findings to the Architecture Board. The integrator will thus study the details on its own.

Add to the commercial contract a general clause that the solution must conform to the enterprise architecture and rely on thorough functional acceptance tests, which the integrator knows and is able to pass. Do not prepare an Architecture Contract as a separate agreement, because it would merely duplicate the commercial contract. The acceptance tests are binding for the integrator.

Leave the architecture of the solution entirely to the integrator, because under a fixed price it bears the delivery risk, and update the ADD after completion according to what was actually delivered. Any conflicts with architecture principles will be resolved only in Phase H as an ordinary architecture change, so the project will not be delayed. The fixed price, after all, gives it an incentive to deliver good quality.
explanation: The Architecture Contract is a joint agreement between the implementer and the sponsor on the deliverables, quality and fitness-for-purpose of the solution; according to G186 it is the main means of handing gaps, specifications and oversight over to implementers. Among other things, it contains the scope, principles and requirements, conformance requirements, stage deliverables, target metrics and the way of cooperation; the draft is created in Phase F and signed in Phase G. Attaching the ADD and ARS without joint clarification (3 points) hands over the specification but does not create agreed and verifiable conformance criteria. A general clause with functional tests (1 point) already failed with the previous supplier, and leaving the architecture to the integrator (0 points) contradicts the purpose of Implementation Governance.

scenario:
Before launching a new portal for reporting insurance claims, an insurer conducted a compliance review against the Architecture Requirements Specification and security standards. The review found that all specified functions are implemented as specified with one exception: storage of photographs and documents from clients is implemented contrary to the specification - files are stored unencrypted, although the standard explicitly requires encryption of stored data.

The supplier also added a chatbot that is not in the specification and sends client queries to an external service outside the EU. The project manager wants to label the solution Conformant because it contains all required functions and something extra, and to launch it next week because of a marketing campaign. The sales director insists on the deadline because the campaign has already been paid for. The chief architect is preparing the Compliance Assessment for an extraordinary Architecture Board meeting. The security manager also points out that transferring personal data outside the EU requires a GDPR assessment, which nobody has yet carried out.
question: How should the chief architect evaluate the result of the review and what should they recommend?
options: Classify the solution as Non-conformant, because one specified function is implemented contrary to the specification, and record this in the Compliance Assessment together with an assessment of the chatbot, which is not in the specification. Recommend to the Architecture Board that the encryption be remedied before launch and that the chatbot be launched only after the assessment is completed.

Classify the solution as Non-conformant because of the missing encryption of stored data, record the finding in the Compliance Assessment and recommend to the Architecture Board that it be remedied before launch. Do not deal with the chatbot further, because it changes nothing about the resulting Non-conformant classification and functions beyond the specification are the supplier's matter.

Accept the project manager's proposal: classify the solution as Conformant, because it contains all specified functions and in addition a chatbot. Record the missing encryption in the Compliance Assessment as a minor finding to be removed in the next version, once the marketing campaign is over. The Conformant classification reflects the fact that the solution contains more than the specification requires.

Classify the solution as Fully Conformant, because it has passed all acceptance tests and the business needs to launch it, and close the Compliance Assessment without findings. Encryption and the chatbot are operational details that architecture need not assess, and the Architecture Board would only delay them. The launch date is, moreover, fixed by the paid-for campaign.
explanation: A solution is Non-conformant as soon as any specified function is implemented contrary to the specification - it does not matter that the other functions are in order and that extra functions have been added. The Conformant level would apply only if all specified functions corresponded to the specification and, in addition, further functions existed. The best answer classifies correctly, records both findings in the Compliance Assessment and leaves the decision to the Architecture Board; the 3-point option classifies correctly but overlooks the risky chatbot outside the specification. The Conformant classification (1 point) is wrong, and Fully Conformant without findings (0 points) denies the result of the review.

image.alt: The six levels of Architecture Compliance illustrated by the overlap of specification and implementation: Irrelevant, Consistent, Compliant, Conformant, Fully Conformant and Non-conformant.

scenario:
An employment office has launched a new system for managing cases of job seekers. Deployment has taken place, internal IT has taken over operation, and the supplier asks for acceptance and project closure so that it can invoice the final instalment.

During delivery, the Architecture Board granted two time-limited dispensations: one allowed a temporary batch connection to the population register, the other a postponement of single sign-on for external advisers. Several planned functions were removed from the scope. The benefits that the Architecture Vision promised (shortening case processing time by a third) are not yet being measured by anyone, and the operations team has no agreed SLA. The office director wants to close the project quickly and move the team to the next assignment. The chief architect is responsible for closing Phase G and knows that the first dispensation expires in four months. The operations team also complains that the architecture documentation does not match what was actually deployed.
question: How should the chief architect close Phase G?
options: As part of the post-implementation review, verify the introduction of business and IT operations including the SLA, compare the delivery with the Architecture Contract and the Compliance Assessments, keep track of the running dispensations, because they do not lapse with the project, and record the removed functions as change requests. Update the repository and the ADD to reflect reality and hand benefit measurement over to Phase H.

Carry out a post-implementation review, verify operations including the SLA, compare the delivery with the Architecture Contract, record the removed functions as change requests, and update the repository and the ADD to the actual state. Treat the granted dispensations as closed together with the project, because they concerned only its delivery, and hand benefit measurement over to Phase H.

Accept the delivery and close the project as the director wishes, because deployment has taken place and operations took over the system without major problems. Postpone the update of the architecture documentation, the evaluation of the dispensations and benefit measurement to the next ADM cycle, when the architecture team will be available again.

Sign the acceptance on the basis of the supplier's final report and remove both the removed functions and both deviations from the target architecture, so that the delivered solution is formally in full conformance. Benefit measurement is a matter for the office's management, not for architecture, and Phase H therefore need not be started for this system. The supplier will thus be able to invoice the final instalment without further delay.
explanation: Phase G is closed by the steps Implement Business and IT Operations and Perform Post-Implementation Review and Close the Implementation; the outputs include a repository and ADD updated to the actual state, recommendations on conformance and dispensations, and inputs for operations and performance measurement. Dispensations are time-limited and monitored, so they do not lapse with the closure of the project - the 3-point option wrongly removes them from the register. Postponing everything to the next cycle (1 point) loses control over open items. Adjusting the target architecture to match the delivery (0 points) bypasses governance and conceals the real gaps.

scenario:
A telecommunications operator is building a new self-service application for customers. The target architecture assumes that up-to-date data on customers and their consumption will be provided in real time by a single API over the billing system, in line with the principle of a single source of data.

Load tests in Phase G showed that billing cannot cope with the expected number of queries, and strengthening it would cost more than the project's budget. The development team proposes creating its own replica of customer data with hourly updates and has already started prototyping it. Two other projects depend on the same API - a new e-shop and an application for field technicians - and their managers do not yet know about the problem. The project manager wants to decide alone, because in his view it is an implementation detail, and the launch deadline is approaching. The chief architect performs architectural oversight in Phase G.
question: How should the chief architect handle the situation?
options: Process the problem as an implementation-driven change request, because it is not an implementation detail: describe the options (a replica with defined consistency, strengthening billing, a cache layer) and, with the support of Requirements Management, assess the impact on the target architecture and on both dependent projects. Leave the decision on a dispensation, or on an architecture change via Phase H, to the Architecture Board.

Process the problem as an implementation-driven change request, describe the options (a replica with defined consistency, strengthening billing, a cache layer) and present them to the Architecture Board for decision. Assess the impact on the e-shop and the field technicians' application only after the Board approves the solution for the self-service application, so as not to delay the decision.

Allow the project to use the replica as a temporary exception on the chief architect's decision, so that the deadline is met, and update the target architecture only in the next ADM cycle. Inform the other projects by e-mail that the API over billing may have performance limitations, and leave it to them how to cope with it.

Leave the decision to the development team, because a data replica (with hourly updates) is an implementation detail within its competence, and change neither the architecture documentation, the ARS nor the roadmap. The single-source-of-data principle is merely a recommendation that must yield to the deadline, and involving the Architecture Board or the owners of the e-shop and the field technicians' application would delay the project before launch.
explanation: Phase G includes architecture governance for implementation-driven change requests: when it turns out that the target architecture cannot be realised according to the specification, the problem is formally described, its impacts are assessed (including a Requirements Impact Assessment within Requirements Management) and the Architecture Board decides on it - a dispensation, or an architecture change via Phase H. The 3-point option chooses the right mechanism but overlooks the dependent projects, which the decision directly affects. An exception granted by the architect alone (1 point) bypasses the Board and postpones the update of the architecture. Leaving the decision to the team (0 points) denies both the principles and governance.

scenario:
A year ago, an insurer completed an ADM cycle resulting in a new document management platform shared by several departments. The architecture is in operation and the chief architect leads Phase H (Architecture Change Management).

The claims settlement department has requested a change: it wants to store a new type of document in the platform - video recordings from drones, which adjusters use to document damage to roofs. A preliminary analysis shows that the platform supports the file type, storage capacity is sufficient, and the change concerns only claims settlement and stays within the limits of existing standards and principles. The head of claims settlement would most like to commission the change directly from the platform supplier and have it deployed over the weekend. One of the architects, on the contrary, proposes issuing a new Request for Architecture Work and processing the change through a full ADM cycle, so that everything is done "by the book". The Architecture Board meets every month and has a simplified approval procedure for minor changes.
question: How should the chief architect handle the request?
options: Within Phase H, analyse the impact of the request and classify it as a minor change by a single stakeholder within the limits of the existing architecture. Process it through ordinary change management, because a new ADM cycle would be disproportionate. Have it approved through the Architecture Board's simplified procedure and update the architecture documentation and the repository.

Assess the request within Phase H, classify it as a minor change by a single stakeholder within the limits of the existing architecture and have it approved through ordinary change management. Do not update the architecture documentation and the repository, because it is a small configuration change and documentation would needlessly delay deployment. A record in the change management system is enough.

Comply with the architect's proposal: issue a new Request for Architecture Work, because every change to an architecture in operation should go through a full ADM cycle from Phase A. Claims settlement will wait for approval of a new Statement of Architecture Work and introduce the new document type only after all phases of the cycle are complete. The change will thus be properly documented in the new SoAW.

Let the head of claims settlement commission the change directly from the platform supplier and deploy it over the weekend, because it concerns only his department. The architecture team will not deal with the change, because Phase H serves only for major changes, and the governance process would needlessly delay a small modification. The supplier knows the platform and routinely makes similar modifications.
explanation: Phase H assesses every change trigger and decides whether it can be handled by change management or whether it requires re-architecting and a new cycle. A change that concerns a single stakeholder and fits within the existing architecture is a typical candidate for change management; even so, it is approved according to the governance process and reflected in the architecture and the repository. The 3-point option classifies correctly but lets the architecture description become outdated. A new ADM cycle (1 point) is disproportionate for such a change and needlessly blocks the business; direct deployment outside the process (0 points) bypasses both Phase H and governance.

scenario:
