Within eighteen months, a bank must meet new regulatory requirements on digital operational resilience: ICT third-party risk management, reporting of major incidents to the regulator within a few hours, regular resilience testing and a central register of contracts with ICT service providers. The requirements affect the operations division, procurement, security, compliance and a number of business units, and dozens of systems including cloud services.

The bank's architecture is in operation and the chief architect leads Phase H. Some managers propose handling the regulation as a series of minor change requests in currently running projects, so that a new programme does not have to be opened. The head of compliance, on the contrary, warns that the regulator will want to see a coherent approach and accountability at management level. Some obligations, such as the contract register, must be operational in as little as nine months. The budget for regulatory projects is approved by the board once a year and the next round starts in two months.
question: How should the chief architect handle the change?
options: Analyse the change in Phase H and classify it as re-architecting, because it affects many stakeholders and the structure of the architecture. Prepare a new Request for Architecture Work and start an ADM cycle whose Phase A will define the scope across all domains; meanwhile handle the urgent obligations through change management so that they are met on time, and record the requirements in Requirements Management.

Analyse the change in Phase H, classify it as re-architecting and prepare a new Request for Architecture Work for a new ADM cycle. Limit the scope of the cycle to technology and security systems, because regulation is primarily about ICT, and leave the procurement processes, incident reporting and management accountability to the individual departments.

Classify the change as incremental and handle it through change management: split the obligations into change requests in the running projects and entrust their coordination to the Architecture Board, which will continuously monitor their fulfilment. A new ADM cycle is not needed, because the bank's target architecture remains essentially valid. The running projects have budgets and teams, so they will handle the changes faster.

Let each affected department secure the regulatory obligations its own way and within its own budget, and update the architecture only retrospectively according to what the departments introduce. Phase H serves only to maintain the existing architecture, not to respond to new legislation, which is the concern of lawyers and compliance. The departments know their obligations from practice.
explanation: Phase H distinguishes changes that can be handled by change management from changes that require re-architecting; a change that affects many stakeholders, processes and dozens of systems leads to a new Request for Architecture Work and a new ADM cycle whose Phase A defines the scope in all domains. Urgent partial obligations can meanwhile be handled by change management, and new requirements are recorded in Requirements Management. The 3-point option chooses the right mechanism but narrows the scope to technology, even though the regulation also changes processes and accountabilities. Fragmenting into change requests (1 point) underestimates the scale of the change, and leaving it to the departments (0 points) abandons governance and a coherent architecture.

scenario:
A state fund that pays out subsidies to farmers is in Phase C of an ADM cycle and is creating the target data architecture. Phase B is complete and its outputs have been approved by the sponsor.

An amendment to the law passed last week newly requires records of applicants' consent to data processing to be retained for ten years and requires applicants to be able to find out online who viewed their file and when. The requirement affects the business processes designed in Phase B (submission and checking of applications), the data model currently being created, and the Architecture Requirements Specification. The sponsor asks whether it is necessary to stop the entire cycle and start again from Phase A. The data architect proposes simply adding the requirement to the data model and leaving the business architecture unchanged. The project office head wants to postpone the new requirement to the next cycle because it is not in the Statement of Architecture Work.
question: How should the chief architect handle the new requirement?
options: Record the requirement in the Requirements Repository and prepare a Requirements Impact Assessment with the affected requirements, stakeholders and phases to be revisited, i.e. both B and C, because the processes change as well. The current phase will decide on the solution with stakeholders; only then revise the gap analysis of Phase B, update the ARS and carry out any change of scope of the SoAW according to the agreed procedure.

Record the requirement in the Requirements Repository, prepare a Requirements Impact Assessment and decide with stakeholders that the requirement will be addressed in the current cycle. Reflect it in the data model in Phase C and in the ARS; leave the outputs of Phase B unchanged, because the sponsor has already approved them and revising them would delay the cycle.

Stop the current cycle and start again from Phase A with a new Statement of Architecture Work, because the legal framework has changed and the existing outputs may be invalid. Redo all outputs of Phases B and C from scratch, so that they take the new requirement into account consistently and no contradictions arise between them.

Let the Requirements Management process reject the requirement by itself and move it to the next cycle, because it is not part of the Statement of Architecture Work. Do not assess the impacts on Phases B and C; the statutory obligation will be added during implementation, when the technical details of the solution are known. Requirements outside the approved scope are, after all, deferred by the RM process according to the rules.
explanation: Requirements Management is a central and continuous process: a new requirement is recorded, its impact is evaluated in a Requirements Impact Assessment (affected requirements, phases to be revisited, stakeholders), and the relevant ADM phase, not the RM process itself, decides on its incorporation. The revision also includes previously completed phases and their gap analysis and is reflected in the ARS and possibly in the SoAW. The 3-point option incorporates the requirement but does not revise Phase B, even though business processes change as well. Restarting the whole cycle (1 point) is disproportionate, because it suffices to revise the affected phases, and rejection of the requirement by the RM process (0 points) contradicts the fact that RM neither prioritises nor resolves requirements.

image.alt: Table of the ADM phases and their key outputs from Preliminary to Requirements Management.

scenario:
An electronics retail chain launched a click & collect service six months ago: the customer orders in the e-shop and picks up the goods in a store. The Architecture Vision set target KPIs - 30% of online orders collected in store and goods ready within two hours. The reality is 12% and an average of five hours. The implementation passed compliance reviews without serious findings and the project was closed.

However, nobody set up ongoing measurement: it is unclear whether the delay is caused by the stores' stock system, by manual picking processes, or by customers not knowing about the service. The CEO asks what architecture can do about it. The head of e-commerce wants to immediately launch a new ADM cycle and design the service again, while the IT director claims that the systems work and the KPIs are the business's concern. The chief architect leads Phase H. Marketing is meanwhile preparing a campaign to promote the service.
question: What approach should the chief architect choose?
options: In Phase H, in the step Establish Value Realization Process, link the KPIs from the Architecture Vision to measured indicators and deploy monitoring of not only technical but also business metrics. Derive change requirements only from a root cause analysis, because the causes may lie in systems, processes and with customers, and assess them in the governance process.

In Phase H, deploy monitoring of the performance of the stores' stock system, the integration interfaces and the e-shop, and derive technical change requirements from the measured data, to be assessed in the governance process. Do not monitor the picking processes and customer awareness, because they are not part of the IT architecture and are handled by the business.

Comply with the head of e-commerce: issue a new Request for Architecture Work to rework the service, because the target KPIs were not met and the architecture has therefore proved to be obviously unsuitable. Measuring the current state is not necessary at all, because the new cycle will start with a new Architecture Vision.

Close the matter on the grounds that the implementation passed compliance reviews and the architecture is therefore finished; meeting the KPIs, promoting the service and the picking processes in the stores are the responsibility of the business, not of architecture. The architecture team will get involved again only when it receives a new Request for Architecture Work with a clear brief from the sponsor.
explanation: Phase H begins with the steps Establish Value Realization Process and Deploy Monitoring Tools and further includes, among others, the steps Provide Analysis for Architecture Change Management and Develop Change Requirements to Meet Performance Targets, with the resulting changes passing through the governance process. The aim is for the architecture to actually deliver the value promised in the Vision, not merely to be implemented in conformance with the specification. The 3-point option measures and analyses correctly but restricts itself to technical metrics, even though the causes may lie in processes and with customers. A new cycle without analysis (1 point) is hasty, and closing the matter with reference to compliance (0 points) denies the purpose of Phase H.

scenario:
A logistics company has its own on-premise middleware as the only permitted integration platform in the Standards Library. During the last year, six projects requested a dispensation to use a cloud integration service (iPaaS); the Architecture Board granted each for twelve months. IT operations now in effect supports both platforms, the security team points to inconsistent access management, and a seventh request is on the agenda of the next Board meeting.

The middleware vendor has also announced that it will end support for the current version in three years. The CIO has asked the chief architect for a systemic solution instead of further exceptions. Some project managers propose simply abolishing the standard and leaving the choice of platform to the teams, because in their view approving exceptions is pointless bureaucracy. The chief architect leads Phase H and integration touches almost all of the company's applications. At the last Board meeting, the question was even raised whether exceptions still mean anything at all.
question: How should the chief architect proceed?
options: Evaluate the repeated dispensations as a signal that the standard no longer meets needs, and in Phase H analyse the change with operations, security and the projects. Propose to the Board a change to the Standards Library (e.g. iPaaS first as Trial) and a Request for Architecture Work for integration, because both the change and the end of middleware support will affect almost all applications.

Evaluate the repeated dispensations as a signal that the standard no longer meets needs, and propose that the Architecture Board immediately add iPaaS to the Standards Library as a full active standard alongside the middleware. Do not analyse in detail the impacts on operations, access management and the future shape of integration, because the projects already use iPaaS successfully.

Continue granting dispensations individually but extend their validity (from twelve to twenty-four months), which will reduce the administration of the Board and the projects. Leave the standard in the Standards Library unchanged, because the middleware will be replaced in three years anyway and the situation will thereby be resolved. The Board will thus deal with requests less often.

Comply with the project managers: abolish the integration platform standard and leave the choice to the individual teams, because approving exceptions is pointless bureaucracy. The Architecture Board will thus be able to devote itself to more important topics, and operations will organise platform support as needed. The teams can choose a platform themselves.
explanation: Repeated dispensation requests are a signal that a change of policy or standard should be considered; Phase H analyses such a bottom-up trigger (technology developments, experience from projects) and carries out the change through governance. Because it concerns integration across the company and many stakeholders, it is appropriate to start, in addition to modifying the Standards Library, a new cycle for the integration area. The 3-point option correctly recognises the signal but changes the standard without analysing the impacts on operations and security. Extending exceptions (1 point) preserves the problem, and abolishing the standard (0 points) abandons governance.

scenario:
A district heating company is in Phase F of an ADM cycle aimed at a new dispatch control system for the heating network. The Architecture Requirements Specification contains a requirement for disaster recovery of the system within one hour (RTO), on which the design of a backup data centre in the Technology Architecture and two work packages in the Architecture Roadmap are based.

After the investment budget was cut, the CFO demands that the target be relaxed to four hours, which would save tens of millions. The head of the dispatch centre disagrees: in winter a four-hour outage could jeopardise heat supply to hospitals. The project manager proposes merely reducing the budget item in the Implementation and Migration Plan and leaving the architecture unchanged, because the ARS has already been approved. The Architecture Board meets in two weeks and the investment committee expects the final plan by the end of the month. The chief architect must process the change. The dispatch centre controls a network to which over a hundred thousand households are connected.
question: How should the chief architect handle the change of requirement?
options: Record the changed requirement in Requirements Management and prepare a Requirements Impact Assessment: which requirements and phases change, e.g. the Technology Architecture and the roadmap, and with what impacts on cost, schedule and operational risk. Leave the decision to the authorised stakeholders, because it is a trade-off between savings and risk, and only then revise Phase D, the ARS and the roadmap accordingly.

Record the changed requirement, prepare a Requirements Impact Assessment with the impacts on cost, schedule and operational risk, and present the conflict to the authorised stakeholders for a decision. After the decision, adjust the Architecture Roadmap and the Implementation and Migration Plan; leave the Technology Architecture and the ARS as they are, because they are already approved.

Comply with the project manager: reduce only the budget item in the Implementation and Migration Plan, while the architecture and the ARS remain unchanged, because they have already been approved. Any mismatch between the plan and the architecture will then be resolved during implementation in Phase G, when the actual costs will be known. The budget is decisive at this stage and the architecture can be fine-tuned later.

Reject the change, because the ARS was approved as a baseline and, according to the rules, cannot be changed during the cycle; any modifications of requirements can be handled only in Phase H after implementation is complete. Recommend that the CFO increase the missing budget from reserves, and merely inform the dispatch centre of it. Such a procedure corresponds to the rules of an approved baseline.
explanation: Requirements are dynamic and Requirements Management processes them continuously in all phases: a changed requirement is recorded, the Requirements Impact Assessment shows the affected requirements, the phases to be revisited and the impacts on cost, time and risk, and the decision on the conflict belongs to the authorised stakeholders, not to the architect or to the RM process itself. After the decision, all affected outputs are revised, including those approved earlier. The 3-point option prepares the decision correctly but leaves the Technology Architecture and the ARS inconsistent with the plan. Merely adjusting the budget (1 point) creates a mismatch that will show up only in implementation, and rejecting the change (0 points) confuses a baseline under change control with a ban on changes.

image.alt: Table of the ADM phases and their key outputs from Preliminary to Requirements Management.

scenario:
A regional hospital has been operating for a year an architecture that arose from the last ADM cycle. After a ransomware attack on another hospital in the region, the national cybersecurity authority issued a warning and the hospital's board lowered its risk appetite.

A security audit showed that the current architecture relies on a flat network without segmentation and that several older clinical systems use shared administrator accounts. The CISO demands immediate changes, the heads of departments fear outages of clinical systems during patient care, and the IT director points out that two key systems do not support modern identity management. The chief architect leads Phase H (Architecture Change Management) and must present the hospital board within a month with an approach that protects both patients and operations. Everyone agrees only that inaction is not acceptable. Medical records must remain available around the clock, even during any changes.
question: How should the chief architect respond to the situation?
options: In the step Manage Risks, reassess the risks against the new risk appetite with the risk owners and the CISO and introduce urgent measures through change management, in agreement with the heads of departments so that clinical operations are not put at risk. Address network segmentation and identity management in a new ADM cycle based on a Request for Architecture Work, because they change the structure of the architecture.

Because network segmentation and identity management change the structure of the architecture and affect many stakeholders, prepare a Request for Architecture Work for a new cycle focused on security. Do not introduce any partial measures until it is complete, so that the changes do not overlap and clinical systems do not suffer outages.

Grant the older clinical systems a dispensation from the new security requirements (until they are replaced) and prepare a plan for gradual network segmentation for the other systems according to IT capacity. Reflect the lowered risk appetite in the Architecture Principles at the next regular architecture review.

Let the security team carry out network segmentation and abolition of shared accounts immediately, directly in production, because it is a threat that cannot wait. The impacts on clinical systems will be dealt with along the way, and the team will complete the architecture documentation once the situation has stabilised. Every hour of delay increases the risk that the attack will hit this hospital as well.
explanation: Phase H includes the step Manage Risks, and according to G152, changes in threats, regulation or risk appetite can trigger a fundamental change, possibly a new cycle; the assessment requires security expertise and the involvement of risk owners. The best answer combines urgent measures managed through the change process with a new cycle for structural changes. The 3-point option chooses the right mechanism for the structural change but leaves the hospital without urgent measures until it is complete. A dispensation for risky systems (1 point) accepts risk contrary to the lowered risk appetite, and uncontrolled interventions in production (0 points) endanger clinical operations and bypass governance.

scenario:
An energy company has completed its first full ADM cycle and collected practical experience at the end of Phase F and during Phase H. Approval of architecture outputs took six weeks on average, because the Architecture Board meets once a quarter. Document templates adopted without modification are too cumbersome for agile teams, and several teams have started bypassing the architecture process. The repository contains hundreds of diagrams, but nobody is responsible for updating them.

The EA sponsor, the CFO, asks whether the architecture practice delivers any value at all. One manager proposes temporarily abolishing the Architecture Board and letting teams decide independently, another wants merely to organise training so that teams follow the process better. The chief architect is to propose how to deal with the findings and knows that another major programme starts in six months. The Architecture Board consists of senior managers who can hardly meet outside the scheduled dates.
question: How should the chief architect handle the experience from the first cycle?
options: Process the findings as change requests to the architecture capability and assess them in Phase H. Because they concern governance, tailoring of the framework and the repository, return with the sponsor and the Architecture Board to the Architecture Capability iteration (Preliminary and A) and adjust the Tailored Architecture Framework, governance processes and responsibilities for content.

Process the findings as change requests to the architecture capability and assess their impact in Phase H. Adjust the document templates for agile teams and appoint owners of repository content; do not change the frequency of Architecture Board meetings or the approval process, because they are anchored in the Architecture Governance Framework.

Organise TOGAF and architecture process training for project and agile teams, after which they will understand the process better and stop bypassing it. Leave the process, templates and governance unchanged, because they are based on the TOGAF Standard and were duly approved in the Preliminary Phase, so the fault lies with the teams.

Abolish the Architecture Board for at least a year and leave architecture decisions, templates and repository management to the individual teams, because approval is a bottleneck. Do not record the experience from the first cycle anywhere and reconsider the architecture practice only according to how the teams fare without the Board in the next programme.
explanation: Lessons learned from the end of Phase F and from Phase H lead to change requests to the architecture capability itself; one of the aims of Phase H is to ensure that the EA Capability matches current needs. If the changes concern governance, tailoring of the framework or the repository, the organisation returns to the Architecture Capability iteration (Preliminary and A), where the Tailored Architecture Framework and governance are adjusted. The 3-point option addresses templates and the repository but leaves the main cause - slow approval - in place. Mere training (1 point) overlooks that the problem lies in the process setup, and abolishing the Board (0 points) removes governance instead of adapting it.

image.alt: The four ADM iteration cycles and the phases that belong to them: Architecture Capability, Architecture Development, Transition Planning and Architecture Governance.

scenario:
A food holding company brings together twelve subsidiaries - mills, dairies, bakeries and its own logistics. The subsidiaries differ in size and level of digitalisation, and some were acquired only recently. The board wants to decide within three months on the direction for the next five years: which companies to integrate, what shared services to create (accounting, procurement, IT) and where to invest in digitalisation.

The holding has a newly established team of four architects. Their lead proposes first mapping in detail the processes, applications and data flows of all twelve companies, so that the decisions have a solid foundation; the work estimate is eighteen months. The CFO, on the contrary, wants to quickly compare the companies' IT costs and choose the cheapest systems as the standard. The CEO needs input the board can work with. The chief architect is to propose how to approach the architecture work. The board meets once a month and wants to receive materials always a week in advance.
question: How should the chief architect approach the architecture work?
options: Define the purpose as Architecture to Support Strategy at the level of Strategic Architecture: the entire holding, a long horizon, low detail. Work with business capabilities and value streams, prepare options for the target state and roadmaps for the board so that it can decide in time, and develop more detailed architectures only for selected areas.

Define the purpose as Architecture to Support Strategy at the level of Strategic Architecture with a broad scope across the entire holding, a long horizon and low detail. However, focus only on the application and technology landscape of the companies and derive from it options for shared IT services, because the companies' management defines business capabilities itself.

Develop a detailed Segment Architecture for one pilot area, for example the dairies, and derive recommendations for the whole holding from its results. A detailed model of one area will give the board a concrete and verifiable example that can be extrapolated to the other companies. The pilot will also verify the approach on a smaller sample and at lower cost.

Comply with the team lead: first map in detail the processes, applications, interfaces and data flows of all twelve companies, so that a complete description of the current state is available. Postpone the board's decisions on integration, shared services and investments until this description has been completed and verified after eighteen months.
explanation: The purpose of an architecture determines its scope, horizon and level of detail: Architecture to Support Strategy has the broadest scope, the longest horizon and the least detail, and corresponds to the Strategic Architecture level in the Architecture Landscape. For the board's decision, business capabilities, value streams and target state options are key; more detailed segment and capability architectures follow for selected areas. The 3-point option chooses the right level but restricts itself to IT, even though the decision concerns the holding's business structure. A pilot segment (1 point) has a scope unsuited to a decision about the whole holding, and detailed mapping of everything (0 points) delivers the architecture only after the decision, when it can no longer influence anything.

image.alt: The three levels of the Architecture Landscape (Strategic, Segment, Capability) and, separately, the four architecture purposes (Support Strategy, Portfolio, Project, Solution Delivery).

scenario:
An insurance group operates in the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary; each subsidiary has its own team of architects and the group has a small central architecture unit. The group wants to build a common customer data platform and shared services for claims handling.

Cooperation so far does not work: each team models in a different tool and notation, defines the same concepts (for example "client" or "insured event") differently, and the outputs cannot be combined. Moreover, it is unclear who is responsible for what - the central unit and the national teams are designing the customer data architecture at the same time, and their designs contradict each other. The national directors insist on autonomy, because local regulations and products differ. The group CEO has asked the group's chief architect to organise the cooperation before work on the platform starts. The supplier with whom the group is negotiating about the platform meanwhile offers to prepare the architecture design itself.
question: How should the group's chief architect proceed?
options: In the Architecture Capability iteration (Preliminary), divide the architecture into partitions with clear responsibility - the group owns the strategic architecture and the shared platforms, the national teams their segments within its limits - and define the relationships between them. Agree on a common metamodel and taxonomy so that the outputs can be combined, and resolve disputes through the Architecture Board.

In the Architecture Capability iteration (Preliminary), divide the architecture into partitions with clear responsibility - the group owns the strategic architecture and the shared platforms, the national teams their segments - and define the relationships between them. Leave the metamodel and concepts to the teams and link the outputs by manual mapping in the central unit.

Introduce one modelling tool, a uniform notation and a common metamodel in all companies so that the outputs can be combined. Do not adjust the teams' responsibilities or the relationships between their architectures, and resolve contradictions between concurrent customer data designs by agreement between the teams case by case. A common tool will also greatly facilitate sharing models between countries and with the centre.

Leave the national teams entirely independent, because each company is a separate business with its own architecture, and abolish the central unit. Have the common customer data platform designed by its supplier, which will unify the requirements of the national companies itself. The national directors will thus finally gain the full autonomy they have insisted on from the start.
explanation: Partitioning is set up in the Preliminary Phase (the Architecture Capability iteration): it determines which teams own which architectures, what their responsibilities are and what the relationships between them are, including the subordination of segments to the strategic architecture. Integration of the outputs of different teams is enabled by a common metamodel and taxonomy, and disputes are resolved by governance. The 3-point option clarifies responsibilities, but without a common metamodel the outputs still cannot be reliably combined. A single tool and metamodel without clarifying responsibilities (1 point) addresses only the technical side and leaves the main problem - concurrent and contradictory designs without a clear owner - open, whereas manual mapping in the 3-point option is laborious but feasible. Leaving the platform design to the supplier (0 points) abandons architectural governance.

scenario:
A bank has an approved strategic architecture with the principle of a single source of client data and the goal of retiring three older CRM systems by 2028. Another team is just completing the segment architecture for retail lending, which builds on this principle.

The project for new online mortgage origination, managed at the capability architecture level, wants to buy a SaaS application that has its own client register - it is fast and the business wants it within half a year. The project architect points out that the application would create a fourth source of client data, but the project manager claims that the project architecture is closest to the real needs of the business and therefore takes precedence. The SaaS vendor also offers, for an extra charge, a variant with a connection to the central client data. The segment architecture team does not know about the project's intention. The bank's chief architect is to advise the project. Last year, the bank's management made retiring the older CRMs one of its main priorities, and the Architecture Board meets every two weeks.
question: How should the chief architect advise?
options: Explain that the project works under the superordinate segment and strategic architecture and must respect their principles. Assess, with the project and the segment architecture team, the options that satisfy the principle (e.g. connecting the SaaS to the central client data), and if none is acceptable, escalate the conflict to the Architecture Board for decision.

Explain that the project works under the superordinate segment and strategic architecture and must respect their principles, and assess with the project the options that satisfy the principle, for example connecting the SaaS to the central client data. Do not inform the segment architecture team, because it is a decision within a single project.

Stop the project until the team completes the segment architecture for retail lending, so that the project has a complete and binding brief. Then select the SaaS application according to the finished segment architecture, even though this shifts the deadline required by the business by several months and the SaaS offer may lapse.

Agree with the project manager that architecture at the project level is closest to the business's needs and therefore takes precedence over the superordinate levels. Buy the SaaS application with its own client register immediately and adjust the strategic architecture later to reflect the actual state. Strategic architecture should serve the business, not needlessly hold it back from quick decisions.
explanation: According to G186, lower-level architecture (project, capability) works under the superordinate strategic and segment architecture and must respect its constraints; conflicts are first resolved by looking for acceptable options in collaboration with the affected teams and, if that is not possible, are escalated through governance. The 3-point option proceeds correctly in substance but omits the segment architecture team, with whom coordination is needed. Stopping the project until the segment is complete (1 point) needlessly blocks the business, even though it is possible to iterate. Giving precedence to the project level (0 points) inverts the relationship of the architecture levels and bypasses governance.

image.alt: The three levels of the Architecture Landscape (Strategic, Segment, Capability) and, separately, the four architecture purposes (Support Strategy, Portfolio, Project, Solution Delivery).

scenario:
Two regional bus operators have merged into one company with 1,400 employees. Each had its own systems for timetable planning, fleet management, ticket sales and accounting, and the documentation is outdated or missing. The depot managers of both firms contradict each other about which systems are actually used and for what, and the depots have retained a high degree of independence after the merger.

The board wants to know the target architecture of the merged company within nine months, because the region, as the commissioner of transport, will issue a new tender. The IT department proposes compiling an inventory of systems itself, without involving the depots, so as not to lose time. The CEO, on the contrary, would prefer to simply adopt the systems of the larger of the firms. The chief architect is starting Phase B and has an approved Architecture Vision which describes the merger's objectives only in general terms. In the tender, the region will also evaluate the quality of passenger information services.
question: What iteration approach should the chief architect choose in this situation?
options: Choose the Baseline First approach, because the current architecture is complex, poorly described and disputed: first assess it and have it agreed with the depots and process owners of both firms - only to the level of detail needed for the decision. Link the target architecture and gap analysis to it and refine them in further iterations.

Choose the Baseline First approach and first assess the current architecture of both firms, because it is complex, poorly described and disputed, and link the target architecture and gap analysis to it. The inventory of systems and their use will be compiled by the IT department itself, without the depots, so that the nine-month deadline is not delayed.

Choose the Target First approach: derive the target architecture straight from the business strategy of the merged company and only then compare it with the current state of both firms. Disputed questions about the use of systems will be resolved only during the gap analysis, when the target is clear and the board will see the result sooner.

Comply with the CEO and adopt the larger firm's systems for timetables, fleet, ticket sales and accounting directly as the target architecture, without further analysis, because it saves both time and licence costs. The smaller firm will move to these systems as part of the integration, and the architecture work can be limited to a data migration plan.
explanation: Applying the ADM distinguishes the Baseline First and Target First approaches: Baseline First is suitable when the current landscape is complex, poorly understood or disputed and the organisational units have a high degree of autonomy, Target First where the target at a high level has already been agreed. The current state is described only to the extent needed for the decision, and iteration refines the results. The 3-point option chooses the right approach but does so without the depots, which alone can clarify the disputed use of systems. Target First (1 point) does not suit a situation with a general target and a disputed baseline, and adopting one firm's systems without analysis (0 points) replaces architecture work with a unilateral decision.

scenario:
A gas distributor keeps its architecture repository on the corporate SharePoint. It contains about 1,200 diagrams in five different notations; for most of them it is unclear whether they describe the current state, an approved target state, or just a proposal that was never approved. Several projects relied on diagrams that later turned out to be rejected options. Projects have therefore stopped using the repository and internal audit has labelled it a risk.

The new chief architect has three architects and a limited budget. IT management proposes buying a modern EA tool and automatically converting all diagrams into it. Business analysts mainly need a reliable overview of the target state and the standards that projects should follow. The chief architect is to propose how to bring the repository into a usable state and how to ensure that it stays so. The audit gave management six months to remedy the situation and will check the result again.
question: How should the chief architect proceed?
options: Tailor the metamodel and taxonomy for uniform classification of content and organise the repository into its classes (Architecture Landscape, Standards Library, Reference Library or Governance Repository). Keep a version and a status for each architecture, i.e. candidate, current, transition or target. Assign content owners and retire outdated items so that the repository stays current.

Tailor the metamodel and taxonomy for uniform classification of content, organise the repository into its classes and keep a status - candidate, current, transition, target - and a version for each architecture. Do not appoint content owners or set rules for its ongoing maintenance, because after a one-off clean-up the repository will be well organised. A small team can also manage such a clean-up within a few weeks.

Ask the authors to add an "approved" or "proposal" label to their diagrams and leave the other content unchanged. Do not change the structure of the repository, the metamodel or the taxonomy for now, because with only three architects it would require too much work, and projects also need a quick and visible improvement right away. The authors know their diagrams well.

Buy a modern EA tool and automatically convert all 1,200 diagrams into it, labelling them all as the current state (for simplicity), so that projects have a single source of truth. The tool will then ensure the consistency of content itself, so there is no need to address or document the metamodel, taxonomy or maintenance rules. Projects will thus have everything in one place.
explanation: A well-managed repository is current, purposeful, accessible and actually used; its content is classified by a metamodel and taxonomy and organised into classes such as the Architecture Landscape, Standards Library, Reference Library, Governance Repository and Architecture Requirements Repository. According to G186, it is necessary to distinguish architecture states (candidate, current, transition, target) as well as versions, otherwise projects rely on unapproved options. The 3-point option cleans up the repository, but without owners and maintenance the content will become outdated again. Mere labelling (1 point) addresses the problem only superficially, and bulk conversion of everything as the current state (0 points) deepens the problem - the concept of a repository is universal and a tool does not ensure order on its own.

scenario:
A fast-growing Czech e-bike manufacturer has decided to adopt TOGAF and has appointed a chief architect with a team of three people. Management needs, within four months, an architecture basis for deciding whether to launch direct online sales to customers in Germany and Austria, which will affect sales, logistics, customer service and IT.

The team plans to create in the first cycle all the catalogues, matrices and diagrams listed in the TOGAF content framework, for all four domains, so that the architecture is "complete"; the work estimate is twelve months. The company has as yet no repository or agreed metamodel, and each architect models in their own way. The sales director fears that the architecture will arrive too late and proposes delivering only a presentation without further outputs. The chief architect is to decide how to approach the first cycle. Investors expect the company to begin expansion into new markets within a year.
question: How should the chief architect approach the first cycle?
options: Tailor the content framework within the Tailored Architecture Framework and in the first cycle create only the artefacts that match the purpose and the concerns of the stakeholders of the online sales decision, so that the architecture arrives in time. Use the Enterprise Metamodel as the basis for consistency and completeness checking, store the outputs in a newly established repository and supplement it in further cycles.

Tailor the content framework and in the first cycle create only the artefacts that match the purpose and the concerns of the stakeholders of the online sales decision. Do not define a metamodel yet and leave each architect their own way of modelling, which will let the team meet the deadline; unifying the outputs can be addressed in one of the next cycles.

Create all the catalogues, matrices and diagrams of the content framework for all four domains, but at a lower level of detail, so that the work fits into four months. A complete set of artefacts ensures that the team forgets nothing, and details can be added in further cycles, once the online sales decision has been taken. It will also serve as a checklist for further cycles.

Insist on the complete set of content framework artefacts at full detail for all four domains and tell management that the online sales decision must wait until the architecture is complete in twelve months. An incomplete architecture could lead to a wrong decision on entering new markets, so the delay is fully justified. Management will surely appreciate getting the complete picture.
explanation: The content framework is tailored in the Preliminary Phase and in individual cycles is populated only to the extent that matches the purpose of the architecture and the stakeholders' concerns; the first cycle is the hardest because the repository is almost empty, and content is added gradually. The Enterprise Metamodel provides a common basis for consistency, completeness and traceability and serves as a completeness check. The 3-point option correctly limits the scope, but without a metamodel inconsistent outputs arise that are hard to integrate in later cycles. All artefacts at a lower level of detail (1 point) waste limited capacity, and insisting on the complete set (0 points) delivers the architecture only after the decision.

scenario:
A bank is introducing a new EA tool and the architecture team must decide how to organise content in it. It has at its disposal an industry reference model for banking and a library of patterns and templates; mandatory standards including regulatory requirements and approved technologies, some of which are to be gradually phased out; minutes of Architecture Board meetings, granted dispensations and compliance assessments; architecture requirements agreed with the Architecture Board; descriptions of the current, transition and target architecture at strategic, segment and capability levels; and an overview of the products and solutions actually deployed.

One of the architects proposes dividing the content into folders according to the Enterprise Continuum (Foundation, Common Systems, Industry, Organization-Specific). The lead architect wants the structure to support governance and reuse and to let projects easily find what is binding for them. The tool allows any structure of folders and content types.
question: How should the chief architect organise the content?
options: Store the reference model, patterns and templates in the Reference Library, the mandatory standards in the Standards Library with a lifecycle status, the Board's records, dispensations and compliance assessments in the Governance Repository, and the agreed requirements in the Architecture Requirements Repository, so that it is clear what is binding. Keep the architectures in the Architecture Landscape and the deployed solutions in the Solutions Landscape.

Place the industry reference model together with the mandatory standards in the Standards Library, the patterns and templates in the Reference Library, the Board's records, dispensations and compliance assessments in the Governance Repository, and the agreed requirements in the Architecture Requirements Repository. Keep the architectures in the Architecture Landscape and the deployed solutions in the Solutions Landscape.

Store the standards, patterns, templates and the reference model together in the Reference Library as inputs for projects and keep the architectures in the Architecture Landscape by level. Leave the Board's records, dispensations and compliance assessments in project documentation and the requirements in the backlogs of the individual projects, where they are worked with.

Divide all content into folders according to the Enterprise Continuum - Foundation, Common Systems, Industry and Organization-Specific - because the Enterprise Continuum is the repository of the organisation's architecture and its structure is binding for the repository. Do not store governance records and requirements in the tool, because they do not belong in the Enterprise Continuum. A structure based on the continuum is also understandable to all architects.
explanation: The Architecture Repository has classes with a clear purpose: the Reference Library contains reference models, patterns, templates and viewpoints, the Standards Library the standards that new architectures must comply with (including regulatory obligations and lifecycle), the Governance Repository governance records, the Architecture Requirements Repository requirements agreed with the Architecture Board, the Architecture Landscape architectures at various levels and over time, and the Solutions Landscape deployed or planned SBBs. The 3-point option wrongly places the reference model among mandatory standards, thereby turning guidance material into binding material. The 1-point option merges standards with reference material and loses both governance records and requirements. The Enterprise Continuum (0 points) is a classification of assets, not a repository, and governance and requirements belong in the repository.

scenario:
A statutory city of 90,000 inhabitants wants to address the shortage of parking spaces in the centre. At a press conference, the mayor announced that the city will become a "smart city" and reduce traffic load, but set no measurable objectives. The IT department is already negotiating with suppliers of parking space sensors and proposes simply selecting the best bid.

The problem involves residents of the centre, merchants, the municipal police, the car park operator and the public transport company, and their interests differ - merchants want more spaces for customers, residents a residents' zone, the police less parking on pavements. The city is unclear about how to measure success or which existing systems (parking fee payments, resident registry) will need to be involved. In Phase A, the chief architect needs to obtain and validate business requirements for the Architecture Vision. The city council is to vote on the project budget in three months.
question: How should the chief architect proceed with the business scenario technique?
options: With the affected groups (residents and merchants, the police, the car park operator and the public transport company), describe and rank the problem, because their interests differ. Document the environment and SMART objectives of the type "by how much and by when to shorten the search for parking", identify human and computer actors with roles and measures of success, and validate the scenario iteratively; reflect the requirements in the Architecture Vision.

Describe and rank the problem, document the business and technology environment, set SMART objectives and identify human and computer actors with roles and measures of success. However, prepare the scenario only with city management and the IT department and acquaint the other groups - residents, merchants, the police and the operators - with the finished Architecture Vision only afterwards.

Translate the mayor's statement into architecture principles (for example "Smart mobility" and "Parking data is shared") with a statement, rationale and implications. Use the principles as the objectives of the Architecture Vision and add measurable indicators only after the technology is selected, when it will be clear what can be measured.

Hold a workshop with suppliers of sensors, cameras and parking applications, let them demonstrate their solutions and derive the requirements from the best offer, because suppliers know the possibilities of the technology. Then write the business scenario retroactively so that it describes the selected solution and supports its approval by the city council.
explanation: A business scenario describes the business problem, the environment, human and computer actors and the desired outcome with SMART objectives; one proceeds from identifying and ranking the problem through the environment, objectives and actors to roles, measures of success and validation of fitness-for-purpose, and the technique is iterative and involves both business and IT. The 3-point option has the right steps but omits key actors whose differing interests are the core of the problem. Translating the statement into principles (1 point) uses the wrong technique - principles are not SMART objectives - and postpones measurability. Deriving requirements from supplier bids (0 points) is a typical "solution looking for a problem", which the business scenario is meant to prevent.

scenario:
An insurer is in Phase C and the application architect has compiled a gap analysis matrix: the rows contain the architecture building blocks of the baseline architecture, the columns those of the target. The service "settlement with reinsurers" is in the baseline architecture but missing in the target and is not marked as eliminated (Eliminated). Conversely, the new service "fraud detection" is in the target architecture but not in the baseline.

It turned out that the owner of the reinsurance process did not take part in the workshops on the target architecture because he was on long-term leave. The project manager proposes treating everything missing in the target as eliminated, in order to narrow the scope and meet deadlines. The head of the reinsurance department has meanwhile pointed out that without settlement with reinsurers the insurer cannot fulfil concluded contracts. The chief architect must decide how to handle the results of the matrix before handing them to the next iteration. The Architecture Board expects the results of Phase C in three weeks.
question: How should the chief architect process the gap analysis results?
options: Assess the missing settlement with reinsurers as a possible unintended omission, because the reinsurance process owner was absent from the workshops: verify with him whether the service was eliminated deliberately, and if not, return it to the target architecture in the next iteration. Treat fraud detection as a new gap to be developed or purchased and record both results in the ARS and the candidate roadmap components.

Automatically return the settlement with reinsurers service to the target architecture as an unintended omission, because the insurer needs it to fulfil contracts, and treat fraud detection as a new gap to be developed or purchased. Record both results in the ARS and the candidate roadmap components; there is no need to verify the target state again with the reinsurance process owner. Verification would only delay Phase C.

Accept the project manager's proposal and mark the settlement with reinsurers service in the Eliminated column as eliminated, but record a risk against it for later assessment by the head of the reinsurance department. Treat fraud detection as a new gap and thereby keep the scope of Phase C within the planned deadlines approved by the sponsor. The risk will ensure that the service is not forgotten.

Consider the gap analysis closed: what is missing in the target architecture is by definition eliminated, and the settlement with reinsurers system will therefore be switched off in Phase G. Select a supplier for the new fraud detection straight away in Phase C, to save time, and record the result in the Architecture Roadmap as a finished and binding decision for the next phases.
explanation: In the gap analysis matrix, a baseline building block that is missing in the target is either explicitly marked as Eliminated, or it is an unintended omission that must be returned in the next iteration; a building block only in the target architecture is a new gap to be developed or purchased. Whether the service was eliminated deliberately must be confirmed by the affected stakeholders - here the reinsurance process owner, who was absent from the workshops. The 3-point option probably reaches the right result, but without verification with the stakeholder. Marking the service as eliminated because of deadlines (1 point) ignores the signal of an omission, and the reading "missing = eliminated" together with selecting a supplier in Phase C (0 points) contradicts the technique and the fact that product solutions are chosen only from Phase E.

image.alt: Example of a gap analysis matrix: baseline building blocks in rows, target ones in columns, an Eliminated column and a New row.

scenario:
A university is introducing a new student information system with online admissions, electronic enrolment and digital diplomas. The previous attempt five years ago failed: the system was delivered according to the brief, but study departments continued to work the old way, study officers had not been trained, faculties did not supply timetable data and nobody monitored whether the processing time of applications had been shortened.

In Phase B of the current cycle, the team compiled a gap analysis that contains only a list of applications to be replaced and new integrations. The target architecture, however, assumes a new enrolment process, a new role of study adviser, new performance indicators and the merging of the faculties' study departments into one centre that will move to a new building. The rector asks how to ensure that the same mistake as last time is not repeated. In addition, from next year the ministry requires electronic transmission of student data to the central registry.
question: How should the chief architect supplement the gap analysis?
options: Extend the gap analysis in Phase B to all sources of business gaps - people with their skills and roles, processes and tools, information and performance measures, finance and premises. In Phase C, also track data that is missing or not where it is needed, because it is precisely these areas that failed last time. Record the results in the ARS and the candidate roadmap components.

Extend the gap analysis in Phase B to people (skills, training, new roles), processes and performance measures and record the results in the ARS and the candidate roadmap components, including organisational changes and training. Do not address data gaps, such as the missing timetable inputs from the faculties, because the system supplier is responsible for them as part of integration.

Keep the gap analysis focused on applications and integrations, because these are what belong to architecture, and entrust the human and process changes to a separate project of the HR department outside the architecture work. The Architecture Roadmap will then contain only technical work packages, which are easy to manage. The HR department has the most experience with organisational change and training.

Omit the gap analysis in Phase B entirely and carry it out once in Phase E, only for technologies, because that is when the specific solutions are known. Business and organisational changes will manifest themselves once the new system is deployed and the study departments are forced to use it every day. Users will quickly get used to the new system, as with most changes.
explanation: Gap analysis is performed in each of Phases B, C and D; in the business domain it includes gaps in people (e.g. skills, cross-training), processes, tools, information, measures, finance and premises, and in the data domain, among other things, data that is not available, is not created, is not consumed or is not where it is needed. The results are reflected in the ARS and the candidate roadmap components and consolidated in Phase E. The 3-point option extends the analysis to people and processes but omits data gaps, which were one of the causes of the previous failure. Limiting it to applications (1 point) repeats the mistake of the past, and moving the gap analysis only to Phase E (0 points) contradicts the technique and the structure of the ADM.

scenario:
A pension company is migrating data on 600,000 clients from an old system to a new platform. A faulty data migration could lead to incorrect account statements and to sanctions from the regulator; the initial assessment (initial risk) rated the impact as high. The team has planned mitigations: data quality checks, trial migrations, parallel running of both systems for two months, and reconciliation of balances.

The programme sponsor asks whether the migration can proceed. The project manager claims that with the planned mitigations the risk is resolved and no longer needs to be dealt with, and the data migration architect proposes that he himself formally accept the risk, because he knows the technical details. The risk management unit has not yet been informed about the migration. The chief architect is completing Phase F and preparing materials for approval of the Implementation and Migration Plan. The regulator has also recently requested information on how the company manages the risks of major IT changes.
question: How should the chief architect handle the risk?
options: After incorporating the mitigations, reassess the risk and determine the residual risk, because mitigations only reduce risk, and present both the initial and the residual risk to the risk management unit and the governance body for formal acceptance within the risk appetite. Reflect the mitigations in the work packages and the Implementation and Migration Plan and continue to monitor the risk in Phase G.

After incorporating the mitigations, reassess the risk and determine the residual risk, present both the initial and the residual risk to the risk management unit and the authorised governance body for formal acceptance, and reflect the mitigations in the Implementation and Migration Plan. Do not plan further monitoring of the risk during delivery, because once accepted the risk is closed.

Continue the migration with the planned mitigations without further assessment, because the initial risk has already been rated and the mitigations reduce it sufficiently. The risk will be formally accepted by the data migration architect, who knows the technical details best, and recorded in project documentation and in the Implementation Factor Catalog.

Treat the risk as the exclusive concern of project management, because architecture deals with the target state, not with the course of the migration. The chief architect will therefore recommend to the sponsor to continue without the risk being further assessed or passed to the risk management unit, so that the migration is not delayed. The mitigations were, moreover, proposed by experienced specialists who have been preparing the migration from the beginning.
explanation: Risk management in TOGAF distinguishes initial risk (before mitigation) and residual risk (after mitigation); after the mitigations are incorporated, the risk must be reassessed and the residual risk must be formally accepted by governance, not by the architect or the project. Risks are then further monitored, especially in Phase G. The 3-point option correctly assesses and hands over the residual risk but omits monitoring, even though a migration with parallel running will last months. Continuing without assessment, with the risk accepted by the architect (1 point), bypasses governance, and refusing to address the migration risk (0 points) contradicts the fact that risk management accompanies the transformation through Phases G and H.

scenario:
At a building society, compliance reviews are done only at the end of projects and few people read their reports. The new CIO wants to abolish them because, in his view, they only cause delay and produce paperwork.

The chief architect has meanwhile found interesting connections in recent reports: three projects independently built their own service for sending notifications to clients, two projects had to work around an outdated API security standard because it does not match today's technologies, and in one project a fundamental non-conformance with the target architecture was discovered only a week before launch. The Architecture Board meets monthly and management wants a better overview of the technical readiness of projects, because two projects were significantly delayed in the past year. The chief architect is to propose to the CIO what to do with compliance reviews, and to support the proposal with what reviews are for. Project managers would most like to replace the reviews with their own declaration of conformance.
question: What should the chief architect recommend to the CIO?
options: Keep the compliance reviews, but move them to project milestones and adapt their scope to risk. Use Compliance Assessments not only to check conformance but also to identify services suitable for sharing, such as notifications, standards to be changed (API security), and to inform management about the readiness of projects; pass the findings to the Architecture Board.

Keep the compliance reviews, move them to project milestones and adapt their scope to risk, so that non-conformance is caught earlier and more cheaply. However, use Compliance Assessments only to enforce conformance with existing standards; findings about duplicate services and an outdated standard are not the subject of reviews and are handled by the projects themselves.

Leave the compliance reviews at the end of projects, merely shorten the checklists and reports so that they cause less delay and projects accept them more easily. Archive the findings from the reviews in the Governance Repository for possible later need and inform the Architecture Board once a year (with a summary report).

Agree with the CIO: abolish the compliance reviews, because projects know whether their solution conforms to the architecture and can declare it themselves in the final report, together with test results and a list of the standards used. The Architecture Board can concentrate on strategic decisions and nobody holds projects up with checks.
explanation: According to TOGAF, compliance reviews have a broader purpose than checking: catching errors early, when remediation is cheaper, verifying adherence to standards, identifying where standards need to change, finding application-specific services that could be shared, and informing management about a project's technical readiness; they take place at milestones and their output is a Compliance Assessment for governance. The 3-point option adjusts the timing correctly but does not exploit the findings about shared services and the outdated standard. Reviews only at the end with shorter reports (1 point) do not address late discovery of non-conformance, and abolishing reviews in favour of self-assessment (0 points) removes independent checking.

scenario:
A passenger rail operator is in Phase E of a programme to modernise ticket sales and shift planning. The gaps from Phases B-D have been consolidated and the team is preparing Transition Architectures.

Planning is influenced by a number of factors: the contract with the current supplier of the sales system ends in eighteen months, the new shift planning requires agreement with trade unions, connection to the national tariff system depends on its launch by the state, funding assumes a European grant that has not yet been approved, and sales channels cannot be changed during the summer season. Partial capabilities will be delivered by several projects in three transition states. The programme director wants a single Gantt chart as soon as possible, by which he could manage the suppliers. The programme sponsor, however, wants to see from the roadmap when passengers will feel the individual improvements. The chief architect is to prepare inputs for the Architecture Roadmap. The trade unions also demand that shift changes not be introduced during summer line closures.
question: How should the chief architect prepare the inputs?
options: Capture the factors in the Implementation Factor Catalog with their impacts (the end of the contract requires a new sales system in the first transition), keep dependencies in the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions, and Dependencies Matrix and, in the Architecture Definition Increments Table, assign projects to the increments of the Transition Architectures. Derive the roadmap and the schedule only from that.

Capture the factors in the Implementation Factor Catalog with their impacts (the end of the contract requires a new sales system in the first transition) and keep dependencies in the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions, and Dependencies Matrix. Then schedule the projects straight into a Gantt chart according to supplier availability, without explicitly determining which increments they deliver in the individual transitions.

Compile a Gantt chart according to the dates proposed by the managers of the individual projects, and record factors such as the agreement with the trade unions, the grant or the summer season in the programme's risk register. Work out the Transition Architectures and their increments only as the projects actually progress. The project managers know the dates of their projects from their own planning.

Do not create the factor catalogue or the increment tables, because they are optional artefacts, and hand the programme director a list of work packages. The dates, order and dependencies will be set by the suppliers in their bids according to their capacities, and the Architecture Roadmap will be adjusted afterwards so that it matches reality. The suppliers themselves know what they can deliver.
explanation: Migration tools serve planning in Phases E and F: the Implementation Factor Catalog captures factors (risks, issues, assumptions, dependencies) and their impact on the plan, the Consolidated Gaps, Solutions, and Dependencies Matrix summarises gaps, solutions and dependencies, and the Architecture Definition Increments Table shows which projects deliver which increments in the individual Transition Architectures. The schedule is only the result of this analysis. The 3-point option works with factors and dependencies but does not link projects to the transition states, so the roadmap does not show when which capability will arise. A Gantt chart based on project managers' input (1 point) ignores the factors and leaves the transitions to chance, and handing planning to the suppliers (0 points) abandons architectural governance of the migration.

scenario:
A travel agency has bought a competitor that sells holidays mainly online, whereas the acquiring company has a network of branches and a call centre. The CEO wants to know within half a year where the capabilities of the two companies overlap, which teams perform them and where to focus consolidation so that the customer experience does not deteriorate during the season.

Process documentation is inconsistent: each company uses a different notation, names processes differently, and the organisational structures differ significantly. The two companies also understand terms such as "booking" or "customer" differently. The IT director proposes comparing the application portfolios and merging the systems first, while the head of quality wants to compare all process models in detail. The chief architect is in Phase B and is to choose suitable business architecture techniques that give management a clear and reliable basis. Management wants to present the results to the supervisory board and needs to be able to explain them to people without a technical background.
question: Which techniques should the chief architect use in Phase B and how?
options: Build a Business Capability Map of the combined company as a stable view independent of organisation and processes, map value streams onto it (e.g. "selling and delivering a holiday") and use an organization map to show which units perform the capabilities. Unify terms with an information map and keep process models only where they add value.

Build a Business Capability Map of the combined company as a stable view independent of organisation and processes and use organization maps to show which units and teams perform the individual capabilities, thereby revealing overlaps. Do not map value streams or terms, because to find overlaps it is enough to compare capabilities with the organisation.

Compare the two companies' process models in detail in a uniform notation (e.g. BPMN), unify process names and derive overlaps and a consolidation proposal from the differences. Do not model capabilities and value streams, because process models are the most detailed and accurate description of how the companies actually operate. A uniform notation will also facilitate future work with the processes of both companies.

Compare the two companies' application portfolios and merge duplicate systems first, because IT consolidation will bring the fastest savings and the business will adapt to the new systems. Complete the business architecture only after the systems are merged, when it will be clear how the company actually operates after integration. The IT director has extensive experience with similar integrations.
explanation: Business architecture in the 10th Edition works with the techniques of business capabilities, value streams, organization mapping and information mapping: a capability map gives a stable view of what the enterprise does, value streams show how value for the customer is created, and mapping them against each other, together with the organization map, reveals both overlaps and the impact on the customer; an information map unifies key terms. Process and other models are created only where they add value. The 3-point option finds overlaps but, without value streams, cannot tell which consolidations would endanger the customer experience. Detailed process comparison (1 point) is laborious and, because of differing naming, unreliable, and consolidating systems before the business architecture (0 points) inverts the logic of the ADM.
